speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We were all profoundly shocked yesterday evening, Mr. Speaker, by the death of one of the members of this house, Mr. Lionel Conacher. Those of us who were present at the annual baseball game between the members of parliament and the members of the press gallery were pleased to see him taking part once more in this popular event, and noticed that he seemed to be in his usual good health and good spirit. His collapse on the playing field was therefore a much greater shock as it was so unexpected.
Lionel Conacher was only 52 years of age, having celebrated his 52nd birthday last Monday. He spent the day with his family and friends in Toronto, but was back in Ottawa in time to play his usual important part in this annual sporting event, which has been a source of so much pleasure and good fellowship. Mr. Conacher was a native of Toronto, and I am informed had been a resident of that city for most of his life. He was one of a family of great sportsmen, and he himself became one of the greatest and most versatile athletes of our time. Canadians right across this country, and sportsmen all over the world, will recall his exploits and will remember him affectionately as the "big train". He received, we know, the honour of being named in 1950, by sports writers in this country, as the greatest Canadian athlete of the half century.
It was in 1937 that he began his political career, having been elected to the legislature of the province of Ontario as the representative of the constituency of Bracondale. While he was a member of that body, he served as vice-chairman and then as chairman of the Ontario athletics commission. In 1942 he was placed in charge of the Royal Canadian Air Force sports and recreation facilities with the rank of squadron leader, and in that capacity made a valuable contribution to the maintenance of morale in the air force in the war years.
Mr. Conacher was first elected to this House of Commons as the member for the constituency of Trinity at the general elections in 1949, and was returned on August 10
of last year. He was not only a very popular member, but he was a very hard-working and effective one as well. He spared no effort to justify the confidence of his constituents in him, and he brought to our deliberations the keen insight, common sense and high sense of fair play which distinguished him outside of parliament as well. Both in this chamber and in the committees of which he was a member, his remarks were listened to with attention and respect.
Mr. Conacher's death came at a time when it might have been expected he still had many more useful years of public service ahead of him. However, he had already made a significant contribution to this country, and earned the lasting respect of his fellow citizens. He will, I am sure, be remembered as an outstanding Canadian, both by us who knew him so well here and by the younger generation to whom he devoted so much of his time and his great energy. I am sure I speak for all members in asking you, Mr. Speaker, to extend to Mrs. Conacher, their five children, and to the other members of the family, our most heartfelt sympathy in their bereavement.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
It was with a sense of shock and amazement, Mr. Speaker, that I learned in Toronto last night of the sudden and extremely tragic death of Lionel Conacher. He had the warm friendship of every member of the House of Commons. I do extend my personal sympathy to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the loss of one of his associates with whom he had been on such close terms for several years.
My own personal friendship for Lionel Conacher went back a considerate time. I had sat opposite him in the Ontario legislature, as I have here. At all times our friendship had been close and understanding. I recall so well the days when he was an example not only of great athletic prowess, but of good sportsmanship in the days of his football, hockey and other attainments. As commissioner of the Ontario athletics commission, he made a contribution to his native province which extended beyond that province. A man can be a good athlete and not always be a great sport. But Lionel Conacher was undoubtedly the greatest of all the athletes this country has produced, and he was one of the best sports this

The late Lionel Conacher country has known. I think that perhaps the highest praise that can be given any man is that he is a good sport in whatever his field of activity may be.
Lionel Conacher was a good sport, and he gave the sense of sportsmanship to those with whom he came in contact as commissioner. It was also in a wider field that he expanded that interest and encouraged young people to take part in the healthy games that give them the physical strength to face the tests of life. I think there are many grown young men and women of this generation who will recall that their interests in one sport or another came from the example and inspiration he had given.
There was no type of sport in which he was not interested. I have one very vivid recollection which shows that it was not only in the hard-hitting and muscular sports, but in other sports as well that he was extremely successful. I recall a couple of years ago seeing a disabled boat in Georgian bay, and going over and finding that it was Lionel Conacher and some friends who were there. He was not in any way downcast by the fact that they were marooned. Instead of that he was fishing-and fishing very successfully-in the spot where they happened to stop. And that was typical of him.
He took life as it came, and took it as a good sport at all times. Every one of us in this House of Commons joins with the Prime Minister in the expression of sympathy to his wife and to the bereaved family, who have been deprived of their father in such tragic circumstances. All of us here today say farewell to a good friend and a good sport, in the very best meaning of that word.

Mr. Speaker, for the second time in less than two months this House of Commons meets with a sense of shock and a sense of sorrow. As has already been said by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), all of us who learned the news last night, whether we were on the playing grounds or heard it over the radio or by telephone, were deeply shocked by the sudden passing of one whom we had come to know and to respect.
When yesterday afternoon those of us on this side of the house looked across the other side and saw Mr. Conacher in his seat as usual, we little thought that this afternoon we would be rising to express the deep feelings of sympathy we all feel for his sorrowing wife and family.
I think one of the really poignant features of his passing last night was the fact that he was looking forward so much to today,
[Mr. Drew.l

when one of his daughters would graduate from the University of Toronto. Surely this is a reminder to all of us that in the midst of life we are in death. Twice in less than two months we have had this sorrow in our hearts.
On behalf of those associated with me I join with the Leader of the Opposition in expressing that sympathy we all feel, to Mrs. Conacher, to the children, and to the relatives of our deceased friend. And to the Prime Minister, too, we express our sympathy in his loss of a good colleague. Mr. Conacher was one whom we knew as a good sport, one whom we knew as a man of independent mind. The house will not mind my mentioning the fact that on occasion I have noticed that he exercised his right to speak, think or act as he pleased. And I am sure that his colleagues around him respected him for that. We all did.
Today on this very sorrowful occasion we extend our sympathy to the Prime Minister and to the Liberal party and, as I have already said, to the sorrowing widow and family, as well as other near relatives of Mr. Conacher.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate the group for whom I speak with the tributes that have been paid this afternoon to our colleague who passed away so suddenly last night. I am sure we all endorse everything that has been said about this good man.
I looked upon Lionel Conacher as a personal friend. He was always affable and kind-surprisingly so, I think, for one who played his games so vigorously and aggressively. I suppose one of the things that made him great is that he played with all his heart, and still was kind and considerate. He was always interested in the sports activities in which I was involved, and he gave me personally much encouragement.
For many years Lionel Conacher has been an inspiration to Canadians both young and old, and has done more, I think, than most people to promote good and wholesome recreation in sports for young people. At all times he set an excellent example.
We were shocked and saddened by his death, and want to be associated with the expressions of sympathy that have been extended to Mrs. Conacher and to the family. And may I also say to the Prime Minister that we sympathize with him and the members of his party in the loss of a very fine supporter.

Mr. Speaker, I knew Lionel Conacher in my undergraduate days, when he was writing his name

in flaming letters on the gridiron. He then acquired the name of the "big train". His later participation in many athletic activities gave him the deserved legendary reputation of being the greatest all-round athlete in Canadian history.
I knew him extremely well when we were members of the Ontario legislature. We maintained our friendship and common bond when we came to the House of Commons as members, and more particularly with our mutual concern for the interests of the city of Toronto. We members from Toronto, who shared a special kind of friendship, considered him a colleague of merit. He had a quick and alert mind, and good solid common sense. He was a man who was devoted to his family and was particularly painstaking and considerate of the interests of his constituents.
He was respected in his native city and admired by many Canadians, to whom he was a personality. As a fabulous athlete he inspired the youth of the country. His contribution in war as well as in peace did not go unnoticed. He died, as he lived, playing the game. All these people, and many others, will be saddened today because the "big train" isn't running any more. To his wife and family I extend my deepest sympathy.

Mr. Speaker, I got to know Lionel Conacher very well in the way one always gets to know one's roommate, and I developed a deep feeling of affection for him. Once you got to know Lionel Conacher you could not help liking him, and I feel that is one of the finest tributes one can pay to one's fellow man. He was ostensibly brusque and blunt but inherently kind and generous; he had an infectious grin and a certain innate charm. Perhaps I might use a well known expression to describe him-he wore well.
Possessed of an incisive mind, as the members of the committee on railways and canals well know, he could analyse a problem clearly and sum it up succinctly. He would go right to the root of the matter. He was essentially a man of few words and always believed in direct, sledgehammer-like action. Thus was this colourful giant of a man.
Much abler men than I this afternoon have paid tribute to his prowess as Canada's greatest athlete. I feel certain in saying that there never will be another name like Lionel Conacher emblazoned across the sports pages of this country. He was the idol of every young boy of my generation. Finally he was immensely proud of representing the good people of Trinity riding, proud of being
The late Lionel Conacher a Liberal, proud of being a Torontonian, proud of being a Canadian. I drove down with him this week from Toronto and he casually told me about the swimming pool and picnic grounds he had almost completed on his farm north of Toronto for his constituents.
Our deepest sympathies go out to Mrs. Conacher and the family, all of whom have distinguished themselves scholastically as well as in athletics. A pall of grief is hanging heavily over this house which will not easily be lifted.
Thus will Lionel Conacher be missed by his family, by his constituents, by those of us in this house, and by his legion of friends across this country.
And so the "big train" has gone on his long, final, inexorable journey.

Mr. Speaker, the leaders have spoken today for all members of this house. May I just add this personal word which comes from the heart.
After a long and quite intimate association with the late Lionel Conacher, in politics, sport and socially, I can say this of our late colleague. Under all circumstances he never failed to be a gentleman. His instinct of fair play and generous consideration of others was outstanding. Though the idol of every sport lover in Canada, the outstanding Canadian athlete, a man who attained success also in business and politics, his success had never deprived him of his essential and altogether admirable quality of modesty.
He was essentially a family man, and the hearts of his wife and five children, to whom he was deeply devoted, and who are a great credit to him, are sore and heavy today. His daughter Diane was to have graduated from the University of Toronto today.
It happened that when the tragic moment came, in last night's game, Mr. Speaker, I was at bat and it was my uncertain hope to bring Lionel Conacher home from third base. A higher power intervened, Mr. Speaker, to bring Lionel Conacher home.

For a few moments I should like to speak about our departed friend. During the life of the twenty-first parliament Lionel and I were roommates. I can say that in those four years never as much as an anxious or an angry word was ever passed between us. Today we as members of this house and many hundreds of thousands of Canadians across the country are paying our respects to a great symbol of Canadianism- I might say, almost a fabulous symbol-of what Canadianism means from the east to the west coast of our fair land.

The late Lionel Conacher
On occasion we discussed instances of amusement that occurred in our various fields of endeavour in the line of sport, and I think it is fair to say on this occasion, sir, that we here today and across Canada pay tribute to a great Canadian, not only great in sport, great in character, great in the open-mindedness of his views and great in the warmth of his heart, but greater still as husband and father of a fine Canadian family.
If Lionel could have chosen the hour when the great Geometrician of the universe was to call him to his last resting place, Mr. Speaker, I do not think he could have selected a more appropriate moment than he did. Because of that we, together with his family, have less to mourn than we otherwise would. We can visualize what a terrific burden it would have been to our friend if the great Physician had decided that he should lie inactive for months and possibly years. Though we mourn, though we are sad, though we are sick at heart, we can for a moment rejoice in the fact that the great Physician gave him this opportunity of transferring from this mundane sphere into the realm of the unknown. While it is still unknown, we are confident in our hearts that the day will come when, on the other side of the Jordan, we shall renew our comradeship not only with our friend who has just passed on, but with all those who have gone before.
Like the other speakers, I extend to the family and to his wife our deepest and sincerest sympathy, and pray that the Almighty in His wondrous judgment will aid them as well as us in this temporary separation. We in this chamber today reiterate all the fine things that have been said about Lionel, and pray that God in His wisdom will give grace and peace to his loved ones to bear the cross.

As one who had the privilege of playing with and against our great friend and Canada's greatest athlete, I wish to extend to his family, to his brothers and to his father and mother deepest sympathy on behalf of the sport-loving people of this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
1.	No. However, on April 29, 1954, a contract was placed by Davie Shipbuilding Limited on Bellingham Shipyards, Bellingham, Wash., U.S.A., for one only laminated red oak keel with five to follow. Laminated keels are regarded as a shipyard supply item, the procurement of which is the responsibility of the "lead yard".
2.	A bid on this construction was submitted by American Fabricators (Canada) Limited, Bynne road, Vancouver, B.C. This firm serves as agent for Bellingham Shipyards, Bellingham, Wash., U.S.A. subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST INFILTRATION INTO GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST INFILTRATION INTO GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are two questions I would like to direct to the Minister of Justice. Has the minister's attention been drawn to a statement made in the last few days by Mr. John Leopold, ex-superintendent of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, regarding the existence of communist infiltration into departments of government, among others, the departments of national defence, external affairs, and the national film board? If so, since such statements revealing the seriousness of the danger, what additional measures does the government intend to take in order to cope with the situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST INFILTRATION INTO GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) for giving me notice of his two questions. The hon. member asked if my attention had been drawn to statements attributed to Mr. John Leopold, ex-superintendent of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police regarding instances of communist infiltration into government departments, among others being the depart-Lments of national defence, external affairs, |and the national film board.

My attention was drawn to an article written by Peter Dempson and carried in the Toronto Telegram of April 23 last. I am informed that this article was based upon an informal interview which Mr. Dempson had with ex-superintendent Leopold. In that article no mention is made of infiltration into government departments. On the following day a more or less similar article was carried in the Ottawa Citizen, written by Mr. Frank Swanson. Mr. Swanson had, I am informed, contacted ex-superintendent Leopold by telephone and secured his agreement to using the material already published in the Telegram. There is a reference in this Citizen article to infiltration and, while ex-superintendent Leopold does not remember being questioned on this particular point, I would draw attention to the fact that the Citizen reference to this item is by no means as positive as the question of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne) suggests, and I quote:
He was asked if he thought communists were active in government departments or agencies such as national defence, external affairs, national research council or the national film board.
"It's possible", he said. "They would be 'plants' or employees who had become 'converts' to communism."
It is on the basis of material such as this that I think the article in he Petit Journal to which my hon. friend refers was made up. My attention had not been previously drawn to the article in Le Petit Journal of May 30 but ex-superintendent Leopold states that he had not been interviewed by this paper. I therefore have no doubt that the item in that paper stems from the articles published previously in the Toronto Telegram and the Ottawa Citizen.
The various agencies of the government dealing with internal security are alert to the danger inherent in the infiltration of government departments by communists and procedures designed to detect such individuals have been in effect for years. I do not think that the casual statement attributed to ex-superintendent Leopold, which merely refers to infiltration as a possibility, need cause us to alter our present practices. The possibility of infiltration is something that security authorities and the government itself have been keenly alive to for a long time.

Mr. Chairman, I propose to

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I have been waiting to apprehend the purport of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. I would remind him that we are not discussing supplementary estimates as he indicated in his opening words. I would also remind him
Interim Supply
that this is not a motion to go into supply on which a grievance can be raised, and that what we are actually considering is an interim supply resolution. I think the discussion should perhaps be limited to questions concerning interim supply.

Mr. Chairman, I used the words "supplementary estimates" inadvertently and I should like to correct the record. We are of course dealing with interim supply. At this stage of the proceedings we are called upon to deal with both. I was quite aware that we were dealing with interim supply and the use of the term "supplementary estimates" was simply an inadvertent choice of words relating to another matter that has been before us.
In dealing with interim supply we are dealing with one-twelfth of the requirements of all the departments of government, and I submit therefore that there can be no question about the propriety of raising at this point a matter that relates to any department embraced in the interim supply estimates. While the circumstance does not ordinarily arise, I submit that in no way challenges the propriety of raising such a matter at this time. I was referring to the statement issued by the chief justice of Newfoundland on May 18 which is reported in full in the press of St. John's, Newfoundland, on May 19 of this year. I wish to quote from the report in the Daily News of St. John's of May 19. Mr. Chairman, since I can hardly hear my own words because of certain discussions that are taking place, I assume you will have difficulty, so I am pausing until it will be possible for you to hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The statement issued by the chief justice of Newfoundland was supported by the other members of the supreme court bench of Newfoundland, Sir Brian Dunfield and Mr. Justice Winter. The reference is to discussions that have taken place in connection with a matter that has been drawn to the attention of the people of Canada over the past weeks and is known generally to them because of statements that have been made in connection with those proceedings. The statement refers to the principle that everyone who is accused must be tried on the evidence produced in the court and there only, and so far as possible without prejudice of any kind. The statement then goes on to point out that anything which would prejudice that trial might be contempt of court. The statement then gives this broad and embracing warning:
We now therefore issue a clear warning to all concerned, and this includes counsel, newspapers,

Interim Supply
radio stations, public men, indeed everyone, that this court will be on the watch for anything which may come within the classification of contempt of court, that is to say, anything said or done in public which may tend to prejudice fair trial, and that anyone transgressing proper principles will be regarded as having been warned and having done it in spite of warning.
I then go on to the specific reference to what was published in the Daily News and I quote from the statement:
The judges have noted in the Daily News of today's date an article under the heading "Judge Dunfield issues order for arrest of Dr. Alfred A. Valdmanis." In this article the statement of claim in an action before this court is published together with abstracts of affidavits filed in the matter. It appears to the judges that there may be a contempt of court in this not only in so far as the conduct of the civil case is concerned but also in the conduct of the criminal proceedings against a person who is under arrest, in that certain of the matters which may be evidence have been published in advance of the trial.
I am availing myself of this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to raise this matter at this time because there has been great concern about the extent to which judges, who after all are appointed by the government of Canada, have exercised the very loose authority in regard to contempt of court proceedings. In many cases this authority has been exercised in such a way that responsible members of the press must have great difficulty in knowing exactly what should be or could be defined as contempt of court.
I need not refer to several recent occasions-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition realizes that I have been extending, I am afraid, too much leniency. He has drawn to my attention that this resolution embraces one-twelfth of the item for the Department of Justice. I do not believe, however, that gives him the right to the same broad discussion as would be the case on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Justice. I was hoping that the Leader of the Opposition would limit himself to a very short discussion or preferably confine his remarks to the terms of the resolution before us.

I submit that this is a proper matter to be brought before the committee at this stage. At this moment we are dealing with a request for the provision of interim supply. We are dealing with a request for the allowance to various departments of one-twelfth of their requirements, a very substantial sum of money. While it may not be customary, on many occasions, to avail oneself of this privilege, I submit that there can be no question about the right of any hon. member, on the first item of interim supply,

to raise a question that is important in relation to one of the departments that is receiving one-twelfth of the amount which it will require for the coming year.
It is upon that basis I am at this time raising this point. I do so because I wish to place before the Minister of Justice in this way, and I submit properly in this way, a situation that I am sure is a matter of concern to him as the custodian of justice generally throughout Canada. I wish to draw his attention to something of which all hon. members are aware, and that is the discussion there has been throughout Canada in regard to the effect that many of the proceedings which have been taken already by way of contempt of court have had upon the freedom of the press. I point out in this case a direct threat of possible contempt of court proceedings has been issued by the chief justice of Newfoundland against the Newfoundland Daily News and, may I add, also against the Telegram in regard to another matter.
I wish to submit to the Minister of Justice for consideration the possibility that in some way there still could be an amendment during this session that would define the basis upon which contempt of court proceedings can be taken in so far as they affect any subject matter under the jurisdiction of this parliament, and I would submit even in those matters affecting the provincial authorities because of the concern of the Minister of Justice and the government with justice to all Canadians. Even if the matter were outside the limited realm of federal jurisdiction, still it would be very natural for him to raise the question as to how the whole subject of contempt of court proceedings might be brought under some clearer definition.
I am sure that the Minister of Justice knows full well, from his wide experience, that civil proceedings are published with complete freedom throughout the whole of Canada. If a veil can be placed over civil proceedings, because it happens that the attorney general of any province decides to institute civil proceedings simultaneously with criminal proceedings, then by that device the justice that is made for the whole of the people through open public trial might very well be denied. I submit that this is an extraordinary statement. This is a direct threat in relation to the publication of civil proceedings because there happens to be at the same time a criminal action pending.
After all, if the attorney general of Newfoundland had any concern about any matter of this kind, there was no necessity to start civil proceedings contemporaneously with criminal proceedings that had been instituted

by the same officer. I think it will be seen that this could produce an extraordinary situation in which the justice of an open trial could be denied to Canadian citizens. I submit, therefore, for the consideration of the Minister of Justice the possibility of examining this situation and discussing the circumstances, by letter or otherwise, with the chief justice of Newfoundland, and of seeking some way in which a better understanding of what really constitutes contempt of court in cases of this kind may be reached.
Here is a case where not only the accused but those who are responsible for the accusations should both desire all the publicity that is reasonable and sensible. I might point out that publicity is an essential part of evenhanded justice in this country. Publicity is a safeguard to the accused, just as it is to those who institute proceedings, whether they be criminal or civil. Unless there is a very clear case of an attempt to distort the processes of justice, then I think that there most certainly should be no attempt to start contempt of court proceedings.
I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the Minister of Justice, that this blanket warning to all citizens of Newfoundland that they must be careful what they say is a unique announcement in the history of Canadian jurisprudence. It is in that light I raise it now and urge the Minister of Justice to give this his careful consideration, merely with the thought that through his wide offices he may make sure that neither may those who are responsible for the prosecution or the institution of civil proceedings have their rights limited by secrecy, nor an accused man have his possibility of freedom in any way impaired by binding a trial in this country with terms of secrecy.

That being so, I am rather at a loss to know what my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition thinks we can do about the matter in this parliament.
