Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to take a few minutes of the committee's time to deal now with a number of questions that were asked of me some days ago when we were considering the estimates of the Department of Transport? Some clarification was asked in regard to a number of objects in the estimates, which 1 had not dealt with, particularly those having to do with increases. I should like to deal with those and other matters arising out of the consideration of these estimates. I was asked for an explanation of the increase of $90,000 in telephones and telegrams. In the statement which I gave on the estimates I referred to the national facsimile circuit established for the accumulation of weather data at Dorval. Inasmuch as this circuit was established during 1953-54, it was necessary to provide funds for only a part of the year, whereas today we must provide funds for a full year's operation, and this accounts for an additional $157,000. Then, too, we must allow for an extra $45,000 for air traffic control purposes in order to cope with the continuing expansion of air transport. These two major increases are only partially offset by the

Supply-Transport
decrease of $123,000 through the sale of the government telephone and telegraph service.
Then there was the question having to do with the stationery item. There was an increase there of $106,000. A major part of this increase is in the meteorological services, because of two requirements, the necessity of supplying special facsimile paper for national defence equipment and secondly, the need of establishing punch card equipment at Toronto for the compilation of weather data.
The increase in repairs and upkeep of equipment, namely $150,000, was mentioned. Approximately $100,000 of that is because we have more ships. We have added the C.G.S. d'Iberville and other ships, and additional equipment repair is required because of that.
An explanation was demanded of the increase of $1,261,000 in deficits. Well, that is due first of all to an increase in two items of deficits. One is $730,000 additional for the North Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry operation, and the other is $581,000 for the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra made quite a lengthy speech and his suggestion was that the Department of Public Works could do a number of things that were being done by the Department of Transport. If the hon. member had given the matter any reflection I am sure he would not have made the speech he did. I say this of course with all due respect to him because I know that generally he spends a great deal of time not only on the consideration of legislation but also on the estimates. I do say seriously that if he had considered the position at all he would not have made the suggestion he did. I say that for these reasons. First of all, let me deal with the major projects which are under consideration in the estimates. I refer chiefly to the Canso causeway. The Canso causeway is a facility that is replacing the ferry service of the Canadian National which has been in operation there for years. It is a facility that has always been associated with the Department of Transport. These ferry services were becoming obsolete, and the Department of Transport determined that an investigation should be made as to what was the best method of crossing the strait of Canso, whether it was by tunnel, high or low-level bridge, or by causeway, and it was the engineers of the Department of Transport, in co-operation with the engineers of the department of public works in Nova Scotia, who considered the problem.
[Mr. Chevrier.l
The point I wish to make is this. This is essentially a water and railway operation with which we, and I say this respectfully, and we alone are competent to deal, and that is the reason why the Department of Transport has been charged with that responsibility.
The same can be said about the Port aux Basques-North Sydney facilities which, again, are part of a railway and water operation. In fact, the Railway Act says so, and the act of union with Newfoundland said that the movements by sea from Port aux Basques to North Sydney should be considered as a railway operation. That is the reason we have done it.
The same argument is applicable with reference to the two tunnels under the Lachine canal. These are navigational projects and it would be impossible to have that kind of operation entrusted to other departments. This is a Department of Transport operation because the control of the flow of water is involved, though I should not be insisting so much on this because over and above that the statute is quite clear. It is laid down in the statute that this is the work of the Department of Transport. If my hon. friend looks at section 9 of the Department of Transport Act, chapter 79 of the statutes for 1936, he will find this, and I quote:
The minister shall direct the construction, maintenance and repair of all railways and canals, and of all other works appertaining or incident thereto, that are constructed or maintained at the expense of Canada and are placed under his management and control.
So that there is no doubt about it. Even if the Minister of Transport did not want to do this and wanted to turn it over to the Department of Public Works the act would have to be amended before he could do so.
Furthermore, why should he want to amend the act? Why should parliament want to amend the act? Because there are in the Department of Transport competent engineers whose lives have been spent on such navigational matters. In fact, the deputy minister of transport is a former superintending engineer of the Welland canal. He was there when the Welland canal was built and there is no other man I know of in any of the other departments who has the experience he has had in the construction of canals, locks and the like.
Therefore, I think it would be a retrograde step to refer to any other department the projects that were brought to the attention of the committee by the hon. member. And what I have said with reference to these projects applies with equal force to projects having to do with aviation.

The construction and repair of radio facilities, meteorological facilities and all facilities having to do with the air services branch are of a highly technical nature and I am sure my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) would agree with me to the fullest extent that this is a matter with which his department is not competent to deal and which should be undertaken by this specialized group.
Again, the matter is clearly set out in the Aeronautics Act, section 3 paragraph (c), which states:
3.	It is the duty of the minister
(c) to construct and maintain all government aerodromes and air stations, including all plant, machinery and buildings necessary for their efficient equipment and upkeep;
There was another matter raised by the hon. member. He asked: "Why is the St. Lawrence waterway being built by the Department of Transport?" Well, my hon. friend knows full well that we passed legislation two years ago authorizing the construction of the waterway from Montreal to lake Erie, either in their Canadian territory or jointly between Canada and the United States, by a crown authority to be known as the St. Lawrence seaway authority. Parliament has authorized that construction, not by the Department of Transport, but by the authority in question.
Then my hon. friend raised the question of tenders and stated that the Department of Transport was now the only department where tenders were not opened publicly. There have been reasons for that in the past. I do not know whether these reasons still exist. I personally have an open mind on the subject. It may be advisable to follow the practice which was followed by other departments and it may be well, at some future date, that tenders in the Department of Transport as well as in all other departments should be opened publicly. There is certainly much to be said in favour of that argument, although there are some things to be said against it.
What can be said against it?

Many things, but I hope my hon. friend will forgive me if I do not deal with them now. But let me say this. Because of the feeling that exists among certain officers of the department I would like to have this matter studied, and I would like to have a committee of the officers of my department look into it, review it, and report to me so that by the time the next session of parliament comes around we will be in a position to make a decision on it.
Then there was a question which seemed to occupy the attention of my hon. friend and other hon. members in the house perhaps
Supply-Transport
more than anything else. That was the question having to do with the Canadian merchant fleet, and questions were asked repeatedly as to what was being done about it.
Well, I do not think that I should be asked to repeat now what I said during an earlier debate at quite some length, and give the reasons for the action by the government in so far as the fleet is concerned. But I would like to put on record some figures and facts because a number of highly exaggerated statements have been made during the course of the debate on that part of my estimates.
Some hon. members have claimed that the fleet has disappeared entirely. Well, as my hon. friend the member for Vancouver-Quadra knows, and as I am sure other hon. members will admit, this is somewhat of an exaggeration. The figures I have up to May 13 show that there were a total of 46 oceangoing ships on the Canadian registry amounting to a total of 316,911 gross tons.
I would also like to add certain other figures because hon. members seem to be of the opinion that that constitutes the entire fleet of Canada. The house knows that is not the case. We have, as I just said, 317,000 gross tons of ocean-going shipping, 181,000 tons in coastal trade, 343,000 tons in lakes and canals, and 479,000 tons in upper-lake shipping, or a total of 1,320,000 tons exclusive of what I am told amounts to about 700,000 tons transferred to the United Kingdom under the transfer plan.
Can the minister break down the figure of the 46 ships into tankers and dry-cargo vessels?

I cannot now, but I will
put them on the record. Now, dealing a little further with that problem, I would not want the house to get the impression that the government has done nothing for the merchant shipping industry, because the truth is that it has done a great deal. I do not want to repeat what I put on Hansard in November of last year, but if any hon. member is interested in the policy of the government with reference to the merchant fleet he can look up my remarks on that occasion.
However, in order to deal briefly and quickly with the position, let me remind the house that we approved a shipping replacement plan which was to allow a measure of relief from the flag covenant. Then we granted the privilege to owners of certain funds held in escrow under the plan to assign them to others. Then for a period of one year we granted a subsidy of $3 million to a number of ships. This was paid to the industry for the years 1949 and 1950. Then

Supply-Transport
we approved of special transfer arrangements which were agreed on with the United Kingdom authorities, with some difficulty. This year we liberalized the policy governing the use of escrow funds whereby they may now be used outside of Canada.
In November I explained to the house- and I repeat now-that if we were to follow these suggestions made by certain groups outside of this chamber and in it we would have to subsidize the shipping industry to the tune of about $5 million. I think that the minimum number of ships that was taken at that time was, say 50 at $100,000 each, which would mean an annual subsidy of about $5 million. With the position such as we see it today, where costs in Canada and those in other countries including the United Kingdom do not seem to be levelling off, there is no way of seeing on the horizon any end to this subsidy. But even that subsidy, were it alone in itself, might be attractive to the government were it not for the fact that even in the minds of most of the owners these ships are obsolete or are about to become obsolete. If this is so, having subsidized them from an operational standpoint, we would find ourselves in the position of having to subsidize them from a capital or construction standpoint. What would that mean? I gave the figure of $200 million. Does the committee think that figures of this kind would commend themselves to the house?
I am not at all surprised at the speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway who, coming from the city from which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra comes, took an exactly opposite view.
He is a socialist.

Oh, he does not take that view because he is a socialist. He takes that because he thinks this is protection. He thinks that the time has now come when we should cease to subsidize industry of this kind and when we should cease to bottle-feed certain industries, because that is what we would be doing if we in Canada were to accept the kind of obligation to which I referred. I am not saying now that it is not possible to give some assistance. I hope that it will be possible to give some assistance, as I shall mention later on. But I do not see how this government could subsidize the shipping industry, to the extent that has been asked of the government by the various organizations that have asked for a subsidy, without subsidizing many other industries.
We have been told that we should increase the tariff in order to come to the assistance of a number of other industries. If we do 
that, I can see no reason why we should not come to the assistance of the shipping industry. However, I am still hopeful that we shall be able to find a method whereby we can be of assistance to the shipping industry. Whether it will be in the form suggested in the policy laid down earlier in November or whether it will be in some other form, I am not able to say at this time. All I can say is that up until now there has been no change in the policy which was announced in November. I should perhaps add to what I have said this comment. That policy is under continual and constant review and I am hopeful that, from the study and review which is being made, it will be possible to assist the industry.
I want to say something about coastal shipping because that is an important matter. It was raised by a number of hon. members. It was said that Canada, for instance, is the only country in the world which permits foreign ships to come in and ply her coastal trade. That is not so. There are many other countries that permit coasting along their shores. In the first place, there are countries such as the United Kingdom, Belgium, The Netherlands, Norway and South Africa which have no restrictions whatsoever and which do not restrict in any fashion whatsoever their coastal shipping. I would not want the committee to think that there is no restriction on coastal shipping in Canada, even with reference to British and United Kingdom vessels, because there are serious restrictions. For instance no foreign ships may engage in our coastal trade but only British ships in the broad commonwealth sense of the word. We have a commonwealth shipping agreement with the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries whereby there is a certain liberalization of trade between those countries. But the opening of our coasts to foreign ships is restricted. Then, in the second place, even among British ships, ships that are not British built must pay a duty of 25 per cent if they seek to engage in the coastal trade of Canada. As my colleague the Minister of National Revenue knows, this duty runs into a substantial amount of money.
I know that my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South and other hon. members here are keenly interested in that subject. I also know that it is a serious and complicated problem, because a number of factors enter into it, such as the shipping interests, the shipbuilding interests, and the interests of trade and commerce. Again there is a certain protectionism that enters into this field. I do not think it is going to be possible to get unanimity of opinion, even

among the experts, unless we give this matter more careful study. I hope it will be possible for me to make a statement in the House of Commons at a later date. I hope it will be possible to find a method whereby we can study the whole question of coastal shipping in this country, the effect which the construction of the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway may have upon coastal shipping, and the effect it may have on the various commodities that move up and down the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river. With that statement I hope it will be possible to allay the fears that have been expressed here and elsewhere.
May I say just one word further. The hon. member for Cape Breton South was extremely generous in his remarks with reference to the Canso causeway and the name for it. This is not the first time the matter has been raised. Then again I think his speech in the chamber has been instrumental in having all sorts of letters and recommendations sent to me with regard to names. I think there is no better name to give to a project of that kind than the name which already exists. While there will perhaps be other recommendations that should be taken greater cognizance of than the one I am going to make, it would seem to me that no better name could be given to it than that of the Canso causeway. The gut has that name. The strait has that name. I think there is even a small port bearing that name. If my recollection serves me right, I think there is a section of railway bearing the name of Canso. That name is found in the whole region. To my mind it would be unfortunate if the name were not carried on in some form.
There is one other thing I should like to say as the result of a remark made by the senior member for Halifax. He dealt with a number of things but more particularly with a matter which I thought deserved some reply, namely, the condition of the light-keepers in the isolated areas of Canada. I think there is a great deal to be said for what the senior member for Halifax implied in his statements and also what other hon. members have implied with respect to our lightkeepers. I remember a statement being made in the house about the lightkeeper on Sable island by the former senior member for Halifax who is now in the other place. The reason I mention it is that during the Easter recess I took a trip on the C.G.S. d'Iberville and visited some isolated spots.
This was the first trip made by the d'Iberville this spring for the purpose of bringing supplies to the lightkeepers at lie Perroquet, at West Point and North Point on the north shore of Anticosti island, and while this was
Supply-Transport
not my first trip to West Point on Anticosti island but my third, I believe, I got a pretty good idea of the life that these people have to lead. I think that we in the Department of Transport will have to give serious consideration to the modernization of the equipment and facilities with which these lightkeepers are called upon to work. Following my visit, particularly the visit I made to lightkeeper Duguay and his family at West Point on the north shore of Anticosti island,
I have already asked my officers to give consideration to that suggestion, and of course such consideration will have to apply not only to the one station but to all stations under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. I am not making a statement now as to future policy. I am simply saying that we are giving the matter careful consideration. I have spoken five minutes more than I intended to, but I hope I will not have to answer more questions.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the general grade level railway crossing situation today. Owing to the rapid growth of many new communities in the dominion, a program that was planned to remove and correct a menace to travel on our highways has now proved inadequate. Instead of being overtaken, the problem is now getting away from us. More hazards are being created with the increase in the number of level crossings and the sharp advance in the tempo of our national life.
I am measuring the magnitude of this menace in the dominion by knowledge gained through familiarity with certain areas, and I am quite sure that corresponding conditions must exist in other municipalities. The continued and mounting toll of fatalities and of the permanently crippled should be given serious consideration by the house. For example, in the municipality of Scarborough, which forms a part of the ridings of Dan-forth and York-Scarborough, four persons have been killed and four have been permanently injured since the first of the year. The question now arises whether this condition, which I understand is being reviewed at the present time, has been handled with the necessary energy and determination to overcome an apparent delinquency.
The majority of the provinces have established organizations for the prevention of accidents in industry and on the Queen's highways. They have set up programs to encourage safe driving, and they have provided incentives to use safe methods and processes in the manufacturing and construction industries. However, under the railway level crossing fund administration it appears

Supply-Transport
to be the formula that a number of accidents must take place at a level crossing before any consideration of the hazards will be undertaken. Their policy is accident accumulation instead of accident prevention by hazard elimination.
This callous indifference to the lessening of the causes of accidents should soon come to an end. Section 265 of the Railway Act, chapter 234 of the Revised Statutes of 1952, provides for the setting apart from the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of $1 million each year for six years, from 1951 to 1957, to aid in the actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of crossings at rail level, on the basis of 40 per cent from the fund, 30 per cent from the railways and 30 per cent from the municipalities, the cost not to exceed $150,000 for any one crossing.
I would ask the house to compare the urgent appeals made by the municipalities that greater effort be made to give them more money from the fund to remove hazards with the amount actually spent. As found on page 19 of the 1952-53 report of the Department of Transport, out of the last appropriation of $1 million only $457,000 has been used. Not half of the appropriation provided was used, and even if the whole amount were used it would be insufficient to give the necessary protection, safety and convenience to the Canadian public as set out in the act.
I now ask: Do you not believe that the municipalities have a justifiable complaint against the board's parsimony and indifference? Here is an opportunity staring us in the face to accomplish a twofold purpose.

Mr. Chairman, may I rise on a point of order. I do not want to interrupt the hon. member. I know he is a new member and I have not interrupted him so far, but I should like to call to his attention that the government referred this whole matter to the board of transport commissioners for study. The hon. member is making a number of recommendations which I am sure are all to the good, but the matter is under review by the board and while it is under review by the board I do not think it should be discussed in the house. The board of transport commissioners has held hearings all across Canada in the course of its highway crossing and grade level investigation. If the hon. member is going to be allowed to make the speech that he is making, I am sure other hon. members will want to do the same thing, and in fairness to other hon. members I think I should raise this point. fMr. Small.]

Mr. Chairman, unless this particular crossing has been actually recommended to the board of transport commissioners and is under study by them I submit there is nothing in the minister's point of order. His estimates contain a reference to the grade crossing fund. It is a statutory item and the only opportunity a member has to discuss it is on the first item of the department. Certainly the minister cannot rise in his seat and say now that because the board is looking into the question of highway crossings nobody can say anything about any highway crossing.

I said no such thing. May I say that I do not take umbrage at my hon. friend's statement that there is nothing in the point of order raised by me; my hon. friend is free to make that statement if he wants to. But the point I am making is that the subject matter raised by the hon. member is under investigation, and in my humble opinion he has no right to deal with it. He can talk about individual crossings as long as he likes. There is nothing to stop him from doing that, but he is dealing with recommendations to increase the grade crossing fund, to increase the amount of payment, and so on. These are matters that have been given to the board for study, and I do not think the hon. member should do that. If he wants to deal with an individual crossing, let him do so. I think he has done that pretty well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is an important point, and I imagine, Mr. Chairman, that you are trying to figure out how you are going to handle it. It seems to me that the point of the rule that we must not discuss matters that have been referred to the board of transport commissioners is that that applies when the matters have been referred to the board for what is in the nature of a judicial decision.
There is no question but that when a matter is before a court for judicial decision, that is sub judice. When the question of freight rates has been referred to the board of transport commissioners, it has been accepted that is in the nature of a judicial decision. I ask you, sir, is a subject matter that has been referred to the board for review a case of seeking a judicial decision?
It is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister suggests it is.
I doubt very much whether you could call that in the nature of a judicial decision. Obviously, the hon. member cannot be prohibited from discussing specific grade crossings, at least I hope not because I have one I am going to talk about. It seems to me he

should not be prohibited from discussing the division of the fund that he thinks should be made.

If I may be permitted one further interjection, I would say it is not a matter that is referred to the board for judicial decision that should determine the point. The point is the subject has been referred to the board of transport commissioners which, in itself, by statute is a court of record. The moment it goes to the board, then it is sub judice.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then, you could refer your whole estimates to the board and avoid discussion.
I do not think we will do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Unless anyone else wishes to speak to the point of order-
There is this one point. I submit the board of transport commissioners is merely making a study and not holding hearings in any sense of the word.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I believe the minister has raised a point of order that is going to be extremely difficult to decide. However, it is going to be my duty to make a decision. That the board of transport commissioners, formerly the board of railway commissioners, is a court there can be no doubt. It is definitely stated in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 251, but in another connection. That matters which are before the board of transport commissioners for adjudication are sub judice is also stated quite definitely in citation 252. It says:
Matters which have been adjudicated upon by the railway commissioners and taken in appeal to the governor in council cannot be considered sub judice while the appeal is pending, because-
Then, the citation goes on to point out that the governor in council acts in an administrative and not a judicial capacity.
I am of the opinion that if the matter is officially under study, whether or not it is adjudication as between opposing parties, by the board of transport commissioners, pending their decision it cannot be discussed here. However, what I do not know, and I am going to be dependent upon the minister and other members of the committee to advise me, is what is before the board of transport commissioners at the moment. My view is -it may be wrong but it is my view until it is overruled-that if there is a general matter before the board of transport commissioners dealing with policy on level crossings generally, I do not think that would 83276-326
Supply-Transport
stop the hon. member from bringing before the committee the special needs of a specific instance.
Similarly, if the board were holding hearings on a specific instance, I do not think that would stop an hon. member from discussing the administration of the level crossing fund generally. At the moment I am in the position where I shall have to ask the minister or someone in the committee to advise me on what it is that is before the board of transport commissioners at the moment. If both sides to this little argument can agree on that, then I shall do the best I can to go on from there.

I have to draw on my memory a great deal, but earlier in this session I tabled in the house an order in council appointing the board of transport commissioners to make a study of the grade crossing situation; of the matters incidental thereto; of the problem of railway-highway crossings in Canada, and to hold hearings across Canada if need be in order to determine whether or not the amount appropriated by parliament for the grade crossing fund was sufficient; whether it should be increased or amended; whether the amount paid for each individual project now fixed at a certain sum should be increased, and whether a number of other things having to do with the whole problem, which at that time and even today is causing concern I am sure to every citizen in this country, should be changed; and to make a report to the government. That is so far as I can remember, but I have not the order in council with me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Danforth wish to add something to that?

Not any more than to say it has probably accomplished the point I was seeking to make, that is to get consideration of this question. I was not aware that the situation had been referred to the board, because I had been continually requested by the corporation of the city of Toronto and the corporation of Scarborough to bring this matter before the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
If the hon. member will bear with my interruption at the moment, I may say that no one seems to have contested the statement of fact the minister has given us. Assuming that the board of transport commissioners is now officially charged with investigating and making recommendations in connection with the handling of the grade crossing fund, I am going to state that in my opinion it is not within our rules for

Supply-Transport
the administration of this fund to be discussed at this time for the obvious reason that no form of political pressure from here or elsewhere should affect the decision to be arrived at by the board.
In so far as any hon. member of the committee may see fit to bring before the attention of the minister the needs of a specific instance, I cannot see that a general investigation into the administration of the fund should prohibit any member from doing that.

If I had not been stopped at that particular juncture by the minister I probably would have completed the remainder of my remarks. I would urge that the Minister of Transport amend the act to provide for a much larger appropriation from the fund-
That is the very matter that is before the board.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sorry, but the hon. member is now doing the one thing which, rightly or wrongly, I decided should not be done. I am going to ask him not to continue to discuss the various types of amendments to the grade crossing fund and matters analogous thereto which are under review by the board of transport commissioners at this time.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. If I were to continue to deal with some specific cases, I would shut off some of the speakers who want to follow and speak in general terms. Therefore, I could leave it until we come to the general item on the grade crossing fund.
You cannot discuss it there, either.
There seems to be no place where you can discuss this.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If my decision is correct, that is also a correct statement of fact. The hon. member is speaking to the general item, and it is not necessary for him to resume his seat if he has other remarks to make pertaining to the Department of Transport.

The problem I have is one shared with the hon. member for York-Scarborough. Within the municipality of Scarborough there are some 82 level crossings that are causing some concern. Of these about 30 can remain as they are for some considerable time because they have not been causing too much trouble. There are 52 of them which remain in the position of needing immediate consideration. The people in that locality are quite alarmed by the
[The Deputy Chairman.]
situation that has developed in the last two or three years with the expansion of their community and with new centres opening up. There are seven or eight grade level crossings requiring underpasses or grade separations. There are 26 or 27 requiring signals and another 22 requiring bank reduction and site line clearance and realignment of grades.
The fatalities there are mounting year after year, and naturally the people are becoming alarmed. They want to have some action taken. Their grievance is that an insufficient amount of money is being allocated to take care of their needs. The action taken to review the situation has taken too long. Instead of having this condition prolonged, they want to have something done about it immediately.
The city of Toronto is in a somewhat different position. In that city there are four or five large projects, one of which is at Pape avenue, another at Greenwood, and another in the west end at Symington avenue. These will cost in the neighbourhood of $800,000 or $900,000 each, and the board supplies only about 40 per cent of $150,000. It does not begin to come anywhere near the amount required to remove the hazards there. The province generally gives some further assistance perhaps to the extent of 40 per cent of the balance, which is required to take care of its end of it. These people are alarmed by the length of time it is taking the House of Commons or the board of transport commissioners to come to a decision to make larger appropriations.
Therefore I broach this subject, as part of a broad discussion of a condition which applies in the whole dominion. I have tried to tie up the local situation with the over-all picture, and I say the minister should recommend that something be done about it immediately, as the review cannot be completed for two or three years. Because of the growing menace in that area, something should be done.
In what I have said I have tried to avoid any contravention of the rules of debate. The matter is most serious, and we are asking that action be taken to terminate this situation.

I should like to say a word in reply. I am sure the hon. member is not conversant with the facts because, if he had been, I do not think he would have suggested that there has been any laxity, either directly or indirectly. On the contrary the city of Toronto has had more grade crossing projects approved by the board of transport commissioners than any other city in Canada. Certainly the amount paid out of the grade crossing fund to the province of Ontario far

surpasses that paid to any other province; and the city of Toronto gets the major part of it.
It had been brought to my attention by the hon. member's predecessor that there are a large number of grade crossings there. But my hon. friend should remember that it is not the department that makes the decision. It is the court. The board of transport commissioners must sit and hear the evidence. Then, having heard the evidence they must determine whether or not the elimination of the crossings is warranted, having regard to all the circumstances. When that is determined, then there must be an apportionment of the cost as between the railway or railways concerned and the municipality.
While I have not before me the position with respect to the particular crossings to which the hon. member referred, I think he will find that the city of Toronto has been pretty well looked after by the board of transport commissioners, having regard to the very small amount of money that is in the hands of the board from the grade crossing fund.

Replying to the minister, I would say that that is just the crux of the whole matter. It is not that I want any greater consideration for the city of Toronto or the municipality of Scarborough. That is beside the point. I have pointed out the general picture, and I am appealing to the committee so that it may place more money in the fund. This would be an opportunity to take care of unemployment.
That is a matter the board is looking into, sir.
But the people can starve while they are looking into it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a moment or two to express my thanks to the minister, his colleagues in the government, and the officials of his department for the many improvements, particularly in aids to navigation, which have been carried out in my own province since confederation.
Most of the lighthouses and fog stations have been renovated, and new machinery has been installed. In addition, in my own riding, two new radio beacons, two new fog stations and several new lights have been established. I am sure my constituents would want me to express on their behalf their appreciation for these improvements.
Although much has been done, much still remains to be accomplished. Newfoundland has probably more coast line than any other province in Canada. The island of Newfoundland has more than 2,000 miles of coast line, and Labrador has over 1,000 miles of 83276-326J
Supply-Transport
coast line, making a total of well over 3,000 miles altogether. Most of this coast line is studded with treacherous rocks and shoals; and it should also be borne in mind that, so far as my riding is concerned, navigation is rendered extremely difficult because of the prevalence of dense fogs or snowflurries during the greater part of the year.
In terms of tonnage, traffic may be very small; but in terms of the number of small boats and human lives involved, it is great indeed. There are more than 50,000 people in my riding, and 80 or 90 per cent of them derive their living from the sea. Human life is precious, however lowly the occupation may be. The saving of a single life more than offsets all the expenditures that have ever been made or ever will be made in the future in this connection.
We need more lighthouses, especially those in the form of light and whistle buoys, which are particularly suited to the conditions on our coast. I understand the establishment of these lights and whistle buoys have been retarded chiefly because the Newfoundland branch of the Department of Transport has no ship at the moment large enough to handle them.
I would draw the minister's attention to the very great need of such a ship specially adapted to and suitable for the handling and servicing of these light and whistle buoys, so that these extra aids to navigation may be provided as quickly as possible.
I have a very special interest in fog stations, because I spent the greater part of my childhood in one, and I always make a point of visiting them whenever I can. In my travels around my riding I have discovered some lack of uniformity in the grading and classification of these stations, and the salaries allocated thereto. I understand a program of reclassification is now under way, and I hope it will be completed and implemented at as early a date as possible.
In conclusion I should like to express my appreciation to the minister and his officials both here in Ottawa and in Newfoundland, for the sympathetic understanding and the co-operation I have always received from them.

Mr. Chairman, the matters one can discuss on this general item are of great importance to the people of Canada generally, and particularly to those of western Canada.
The matter of freight rates across the nation has always been a very important subject, and has usually been contentious. A royal commission inquired into the general freight rate structure and the general freight rate policy, and a report was made in 1951.

Supply-Transport
Since then the board of transport commissioners has been endeavouring to carry out the recommendations made by the royal commission on transportation. The recommendations of that royal commission could be summed up in one sentence, namely, support of the principle of equalization of freight rates.
Since that time the board of transport commissioners has taken steps toward equalizing freight rates across the country. Those of us who come from western Canada particularly are very grateful for the extent of equalization that has been brought about. As the minister himself pointed out on an earlier occasion, the class rates have been made more equal by a reduction of 5 per cent in western Canada and an increase of 10 per cent in eastern Canada. The question of transcontinental rates was dealt with by the commission in the one and one-third rule, and that has been of benefit to the people on the prairies.
Another of the recommendations was the $7 million subsidy to help bear the cost of maintenance of railways in that area of northern Ontario that has so little revenue-producing freight. The step in providing the $7 million subsidy was a very important departure from general policy up to that time. I should like to point out to the minister that the benefit he told us had resulted from the $7 million subsidy, namely, a reduction in east-west rates by about 8 per cent, can easily be taken away by action in some other way or by action in another department.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that since this subsidy was inaugurated there has been a reduction of 7 cents a bushel on grain coming through Fort William and Port Arthur.'That is equalization in reverse. That, in my judgment, is the very opposite type of policy to that which was set forth in the recommendation for the payment of the subsidy; and if one multiplies the 7 cents a bushel with the quantity of grain coming through that route, it is easy to see that the result is a cost to the prairies more than twice as great as the benefit coming from the $7 million subsidy.
One of the things that has disturbed me over the last few weeks and months is the continuing suggestion by people in responsible positions that there may be a change in the Crowsnest pass rates. I should like the minister to assure us that no consideration is being given to a change in those rates that would result in an increased burden on the people of western Canada. One of the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation was that the Crowsnest pass rates

should not be tampered with. Since that time, as was pointed out in the Financial Times of May 21, the board of transport commissioners on February 15 referred to-and this is in quotation marks-the abnormally low statutory rates on western export. The writer of this article, whether he has reason for his speculation or not, goes on to say that consideration is being given to a change in the Crowsnest pass rates. I am hopeful that the minister will give the committee and western Canada the assurance now that no such change is contemplated.
In his recent address to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway at the annual meeting, the president, Mr. W. A. Mather, dealt at some length with the question of the Crowsnest pass rates, and as one would expect, he criticized them very severely. I think his criticism was well answered by the minister at page 3124 of Hansard of this session when he said:
The railway business is dependent upon the general activity in transportation services in the country as a whole.
Therefore, any drop there may be in revenue for the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. is not because we have the Crowsnest pass rates, but merely and solely because there has been a drop in general freight revenue. It is easy to see the advantage of the Crowsnest pass rates in western Canada when one compares, for example, the lake freight rate for the shipment of grain that prevailed in 1936 with the rate that prevails today. In 1936 the rate was 4-J cents per bushel; the lake freight rate today is 14J cents per bushel. The rate has increased three times since 1936. This increase in lake freight rates and in ocean freight rates has meant a lower price to the producers of grain. In the face of these other very substantial increases in the cost of moving grain to the markets of the world, I am hopeful that the government will continue its present policy of maintaining intact the present Crowsnest pass rates, and will resist the pressure that is being placed on them apparently by the railway companies, the C.P.R. in particular, and will say no to any suggestion that the Crowsnest pass rates be increased.
As I have said, I believe the minister pointed out very well the reason for any decrease at the present time in railway revenues, namely, the decrease in the general freight traffic. As a matter of fact, any time that the railways have hauled higher than average quantities of grain at the so-called low Crowsnest pass rates, in those periods of time the railway companies have made their largest profits. Nothing will convince

the people of western Canada that any tampering with the Crowsnest pass rates is justified.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I am hopeful that the minister will quell those rumours now and give us the assurance that no consideration is being given to a change in those rates.

At the outset I should like
to express my appreciation to the minister of what he said a few moments ago with respect to his trip along the coast and the reaction that he got to the services being rendered by lighthouse keepers at various isolated communities, of which we all know.
1 am sure it is an expression that will meet with the approval of the public generally. It is something which is tardy in recognition, and I am very glad that the minister has taken the position to express the views which he did this afternoon.
The other night the senior member for Halifax referred in some detail to facilities at the port of Halifax. Since he represents the city of Halifax, this naturally comes especially within his prerogative. But Halifax is also the great port of the province of Nova Scotia, one in which we all have a great interest, and I want to refer for a moment-and I shall speak only briefly-to the situation as it exists there.
Everyone knows that the port of Halifax is one of our great winter ports. It has also developed a very great summer import trade as well, because Halifax is a port of call for New York ships and others and there has been a demand for increased facilities there.
During the last year or so we have had a situation where the ships have had to lie in the stream for as long, I am told, as three days before obtaining dockage facilities in order to unload. Needless to say, shipping lying in the stream is an expensive matter; it can amount to as much as several thousand dollars a day. In order to cope with that situation we require additional facilities. I believe when the port was first envisaged many years ago there was a provision made in the old blueprint for the construction of pier A as a sort of twin to the existing pier we have there now. I know that that matter has been brought to the attention of the minister by the voluntary commission representing the business interests in Halifax, and I hope the minister and his department will be able to provide funds in the estimates so that construction can be commenced on that project in the very near future.
As the minister knows, pier 34, which we have there now, was considered to be a temporary structure but it lasted for a very long
Supply-Transport
time until a locomotive engineer became exasperated and drove his engine right through so that it went right through the floor and by the time it was dug up the foundations had been irreparably damaged.
Now we are deprived of pier 34 and we have additional shipping to handle and we require not only an additional pier but the present pier facilities extended and the building of additional sheds. In fact a long-term project should now be brought forward for the development of the port of Halifax, and I simply want to put myself on record as being thoroughly in accord with that. I hope that the minister, with the speed with which he is known to act, particularly when he knows that he has public opinion behind him, will examine these matters and push through the completion of this project.
Although it is true that imports through Halifax port have been increasing yet I think the situation with respect to exports of Canadian goods through Canadian ports is not entirely a happy one. The minister has already heard me speak on this subject and I know he has said: "Well, what can I do about it?" That is the question, and if he asked me now I do not know that I would be in a position to give him a categorical answer, but I know he is cognizant of the problem and I would urge him and his departmental officials to do all in their power to improve the situation.
Two years ago I put the figures on the record with regard to the export of Canadian goods through Canadian ports and I do not want to repeat these now. But I have one or two cases which are a striking illustration of the situation and I would like to put them on record.
For example, though we only have official figures up to 1952, it can be shown that in 1950 the number of Canadian automobiles exported through American ports amounted to 23,046 and the number exported through Canadian ports for the same year amounted to 11,227, or roughly in proportion two to one. That means in effect that for every car exported from Canada two went through an American port for every one that went through a Canadian port. I will not put the figures for 1951 on record but the proportion amounted to five to one which means that for every five cars exported through American ports only one went through Canadian ports.
In 1952, 71,361 cars were exported through American ports and 8,406 through Canadian ports or a proportion of nine to one. If you want to consider automobile parts in 1950 it will be seen that more were shipped through Canadian ports than through American ports, but in 1951 the proportion was

Supply-Transport
two to one through American ports and in 1952 the proportion was three-and-a-half to one in favour of the American ports.
The same thing can be said as regards farm machinery. The figures are almost exactly the same for there was a proportion of one-and-a-half to one through Canadian ports in 1950 and over five to one in favour of American ports in 1952.
Now, I know one can say, "well, that is business. What can we do about it. Do you suggest we bludgeon business into moving freight through Canadian ports?" I am not suggesting that, but I do suggest that some steps could be taken.
The automobile industry is an example of one which is prospering greatly through a national policy of which I do not complain, but I do say that a national policy should work both ways and if industry can prosper under such a policy then that industry should utilize Canadian ports and Canadian facilities as far as possible so that we may be able to build up a balanced economy.
It is a rather striking thing that other industries have apparently been able to use Canadian ports. For example, the International Nickel Company which, I imagine, is as well-managed as any other company, has increased its exports through Canadian ports to a striking degree during 1951-52. They have not found it necessary to use American ports. In addition, the great paper industries export through the Canadian ports and their exports recently went up from
3,900,000	hundredweight in 1950 to 8,819,000 hundredweight in 1952.
Some of these, of course, depend on port facilities and the places to which the goods are being exported, but if Canadian industry generally can find it profitable and advantageous in their international trade to use Canadian ports then I think that some fairly strenuous suggestion should be made to some of the other companies which for some reason have not seen fit to use Canadian ports and in fact almost ignore them completely.
The minister some time ago, and the hon. member for Halifax the other night, mentioned the work done by the department in maintaining the Canadian National steamship freighters and we are glad that that has been done. The old "Lady" boats were probably obsolescent, but they served a useful purpose and we are glad to see that Canadian National freighters are still operating, and that the minister has been able to play a part in their maintenance under the aegis of his department.
However, I do think these facilities should be extended. After all, if we are going to develop this nation, the outer periphery of
[Mr. Nowlan.l
it as well as the centre, then the government must spend money even if it means subsidization in order to build up our economy.
In this connection I am thinking particularly of the maritimes and the shipment of agricultural goods to, we will say, Venezuela which is a country on the gold standard and therefore without any dollar exchange problem. Venezuela, for instance, would like to buy through Nova Scotia anything up to
3,000	or 3,500 cases of eggs per week. The market is there, indeed a very considerable market, and what we require now are steamships and refrigerating services which can be operated through the port of Halifax direct to Venezuela. As it is today the progressive producers are going as far as they possibly can and adopting methods of transshipment sometimes through the port of New York, unloading them there by truck, and then putting them on ships through American harbours and shipping them to Venezuela. That has been done with several carloads within the last few months and it justifies the existence of that market but it is only an indication of what could be done if additional facilities were provided and we could ship direct to South American and West Indies ports generally, for these markets are of great value to the maritimes.
I think there are real opportunities for development there. We need regular services for freight, including refrigerator services, as well as passenger services. The Canadian National Railways have pioneered services through there to a certain extent and I can appreciate the fact that there have been great difficulties in so doing but a trade such as this is something that should be extended.
The minister will probably find that from an operating standpoint there would be a deficit on the first year. I do not know about that, but I do know that the money would be returned to the national economy. On balance it would be very much worth while and an expenditure which I think is more than justified.
To revert again to Halifax for a moment, when the minister was raising the point of order with my hon. friend about the grade crossings a little while ago I was reminded of another matter that I do not think comes within the jurisdiction of the transport commission and I doubt whether it comes within the grade crossing fund. However, I know it is a matter which has been brought to the minister's attention. I am sure it is going to be brought to his attention and to that of other ministers in the immediate future. I refer to the drastic situation which the people of Halifax face in so far as so-called bottlenecks are concerned.

The minister knows full well of the situation at Halifax, which is situated on a peninsula, where two main arteries coming out of there both have railway crossings. If something were to happen there, such as a bomb being dropped, you could have possibly
100,000	to 150,000 people sealed off thereby. So far as the Minister of Transport is concerned, while it may be a matter for civilian defence, it comes to a certain extent within his purview with respect to grade crossings. It is a matter which is attracting a great deal of attention at the moment. Halifax is certainly a city where, unfortunately, if we were ever to find ourselves in another war the people would be in a most vulnerable position. Even with regard to the explosions which took place in the dockyard at the end of the last war, in that city there was created a situation which could easily have got out of control. It is beyond the scope of the municipality and of the province. It is a matter which, as I said, must be dealt with. I believe it will be under review in the not too distant future. I mention it now as something which concerns not only the city but the province as a whole.
Much has been said about the Canadian mercantile marine. I notice that the minister said this afternoon that he hoped that some time in the near future-I gathered it might perhaps be before this house rose or at some early date-he will be in a position to make a general statement, in view of the development of the St. Lawrence waterway, with regard to the whole situation.

May I just make it clear that the statement I had in mind concerned the restrictions on coastal trade and not on the other matter, although I said that the other matter was under review. I do not want to be misunderstood.

I thank the minister for what he has said. With respect to coastal trade the situation is a difficult one. I realize that the co-operation, shall we say, with regard to commonwealth and British ships along the coast is a matter of policy which is to be reviewed in the over-all picture. It is possible that the minister will say that this criticism is not well founded. I have drawn it to his attention before and I have had it drawn to my attention again by captains in the coastal trade who, rightly or wrongly, believe this and I believe some explanation should be given. They complain of the fact that the other boats coming in-British boats -do not have to comply with the provision of the steamship inspection act, whereas they are obliged to do so. They contend that the cost of that inspection service, having regard

to the relatively small amount of revenue which they derive from their annual business, puts them in a most unfortunate position regardless of the difference in salaries and other costs and operating expenses. One captain told me that in his boat the costs made a difference of $10,000 a year, in connection with his complying with that inspection service. Their argument there is that if other boats take part in the coastal service, then at least they should be in the same situation and under the same regulations, and that if others are not forced to comply with these regulations, they should not be obliged to do so.
Speaking of the steamship inspection service, Mr. Chairman, I should like to express my appreciation again to the minister-I do not want to be too thankful and too complimentary this afternoon-for the co-operation he showed in a matter which I raised. Under the provisions of the act I think unfortunately -at least I say that I did not notice it in the act or I would have questioned it at the time-a certain situation has arisen. Now boats of over 15 tons come within the provisions of this inspection act. In Nova Scotia we have had a situation where small fishing boats, motor boats, just over 15 tons have been ordered ashore. Sometimes they have been ordered ashore even at the busiest season of the year, and have been told that they have had to undergo renovations and repairs running into thousands of dollars before they can operate again. I must say that when one particular instance was brought to the attention of the minister he acted most co-operatively and at least avoided any injustice being done for the particular season and permitted the boats to continue operating. Otherwise they would have lost practically all the money they would have earned that year.
I think that provision is too far-reaching. I hope the minister will at least have the regulations relaxed in so far as the statute permits. After all, these men going out in these little fishing boats-they, their fathers and their grandfathers have been doing it for three generations-do not intend to drown themselves or get drowned. They go out in the morning and come back at night. I am speaking now of the small fishing boats on the Nova Scotia coast. Their fathers did it and their grandfathers did it. They do not think they have to have lifeboats with copper water tanks and a whole lot of the other things they might need if they were carrying passengers or were pleasure boats or were going out to sea for two or three days. They have shafts in their motor boats of 3f inches. These motor boats with these shafts have carried them and their fathers back and forth

Mr. Chairman, earlier in the session I placed on the order paper a resolution calling for the increasing of elevator space and port facilities at Churchill, but before I had a chance to have this resolution debated the minister was kind enough to announce that the facilities were being

doubled. At this very late date I must thank him for such prompt action. I may say that his announcement was made just prior to Christmas. It so happened that I had made a tour from Churchill through Hudson bay to the United Kingdom last fall, and some of my friends were kind enough to give me credit for the announcement. Members of the house who know how difficult it is to get the government to accept resolutions even when we have very good arguments will know that I cannot claim the credit for this decision.
I do not expect that during my lifetime Churchill will become as large as Montreal, Halifax or Vancouver, but the Canadian people have an investment of over $50 million in the railway and the harbour facilities and I think it is in the interests of Canada that we give this development a fair chance. I must express my appreciation to the minister for the sympathetic consideration which has been given since he took over the department. Some years ago we had a Saskatchewan homesteader in the person of Mr. Dunning as minister of transport, but although he was from Saskatchewan I do not think he gave Churchill and the Hudson bay route the sympathetic consideration that the present minister has.
However, there is one matter that I should like to bring to the minister's attention. On the 18th of February his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, announced a differential that is really going to place Churchill at a great disadvantage. As of the 18th of February wheat was being offered at Fort William at $1.79, at Vancouver at $1.86 and at Churchill at $1.88. It was not possible in February for wheat to be sold for immediate delivery out of Churchill, and the minister did indicate that the matter would be reviewed later. I think he will appreciate my position as a farmer at Sturgis. Some of our wheat moves to Churchill and some to Fort William. Wheat moves to Churchill at an 18 cent rate and at a 20 cent rate to Fort William. I think it is unreasonable for the wheat board to offer wheat moved from Sturgis at a price of $1.88 at Churchill and $1.79 at Fort William.
I know it is an accident that the Minister of Trade and Commerce happens to come from Port Arthur, but it is a fact that he does come from there and I want to suggest to the Minister of Transport that he keep a very watchful eye on the price at which wheat is offered at Churchill when ships are in a position to move in and out of the port. As I intimated earlier, I travelled from Churchill to London on the S.S. Begonia. The captain of the ship had come into the

port of Churchill on half a dozen occasions, and with radar, the gyrocompass and the excellent aids to navigation provided by the Department of Transport Captain Reekie indicated that it was quite safe to go into Churchill, that it was no more hazardous than to go into Montreal.
I think there are two things that are important. I think we should have more cargo coming into Churchill so that the people who live on the plains may have the advantage of the short rail haul and be able to get goods from overseas markets by the most direct route. As I said, we want to make sure that the increased facilities will be used to capacity. I have one further suggestion which I think will provide a little additional revenue. I do not expect that in the very near future there will be a large volume of passenger traffic through Churchill, but most of the ships that come there have accommodation for some passengers. The cargo ships that move out of Halifax and Montreal carry a great many people who prefer to travel on cargo ships because they get away from the noise and crowds of the passenger ships.
Last year I found it very difficult to get information as to what ships might be sailing, when they would be sailing and whether or not there would be accommodation. It so happens that the railway line from The Pas to Churchill is operated by a separate branch of the Canadian National Railways. The C.N.R. employees where I live are very co-operative but they did not seem to have information as to when ships were sailing and whether there would be accommodation. In my opinion it would not cost very much to have a better liaison between the national harbours board at Churchill, the Hudson bay branch of the railway and the Canadian National Railways. If a ship were coming into Churchill with accommodation for ten passengers that information could be made available to the C.N.R. passenger agency in Winnipeg and in turn to their branch agencies throughout the west.
As I said, I do not expect that there will be thousands of people wanting to travel by way of Churchill, but having crossed the Atlantic on several occasions by way of Montreal may I say-and I do not think I could be accused of being partial-that I never enjoyed an ocean voyage more than the restful trip from Churchill to London, England, which took seventeen days. Therefore I hope the minister will be able to make arrangements so that Canadian National Railways can make available to prospective travellers information as to the cost and the possible dates that ships may be sailing from Churchill.

I am somewhat concerned about the question raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia with respect to the Crowsnest rates. I am a little bit afraid that some of the opponents of those rates may say that only one or two members of the House of Commons made any protest against changing them. Of course the reason that only one or two members are protesting is the fact that no measure is before the house proposing a change in these rates. On the other hand, I am satisfied if any measure were brought in to make a change in the Crowsnest rates every member from the prairie provinces would rise and protest, and I think that we can promise the minister one of the bitterest fights the house has seen for many years if such a measure is introduced. The hon. member for Assiniboia asked the minister to give the house the assurance that the government is not considering any change in these rates. I think we would appreciate getting that assurance from the minister-
It will not be difficult.
-because we could not hear what he said before. To us he seemed to be whispering. I wish he would give us that assurance in a more audible voice at this time and in that way save a lot of debate.

I can tell my hon. friend immediately that he can cease worrying at once because there is nothing before the house, nothing before the government and certainly no change in the position which I announced earlier so far as the Crowsnest rates are concerned. I do not know what may have brought this about other than the fact that the railways may be losing money on the movement of grain through the Crowsnest pass. I mean comparatively speaking in so far as the rates for the movement of grain elsewhere are concerned.
But actually there is no loss of money on the transportation, is there?

I asked my officers to get a statement I have in my office. With it I could have dealt with the matter more intelligently, but unfortunately I am not able to get my hands on it. Perhaps that is the basis for the fear that hon. members have in their minds. I hope that I can put something on the record at a later date. In any event, even if that were the position and it was found necessary to give some attention to the problem, there is certainly no intention of amending the act. Certainly no consideration has ever been given by the government to amending the act. If that will allay the fears of my hon. friends, I am happy to give that assurance right now.

Supply-Transport

I was extremely interested, Mr. Chairman, this afternoon in hearing some of the remarks of the Minister of Transport concerning the jurisdiction which he and his department had over the canal system of Canada, and the deft way in which he made it quite obvious to us that he and his department controlled the canals of Canada. It brought to my mind the desire of those of us on this side of the house to have an excellent corps of people behind us to do research, to dig out facts and to develop arguments so that we could always be as accurate as the minister.
I had a little premonition that perhaps the statement was not technically and completely correct. I know the minister felt it was. I went upstairs, and the first thing I did was to look up the item in the act that gives him the power. The item is very definite and says that the minister shall have the management, charge and direction of all government railways and canals, and of all works and property appertaining or incident to such railways and canals, etc. Then, I leafed through the first 786 pages of the Canada Year Book looking for something I had seen there before and I found this at the top of page 786:
Under the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Public Works are the St. Andrews lock (length, width and draught, respectively, 215, 45 and 17 feet) at Selkirk on the Red river, Manitoba, and the lock at Poupore, Quebec.
I mention this not really to niggle away at the minister at all, but just to point out how easy it is for even experts like the Department of Transport to lose a lock in a canal, and to tell us that everything comes under their jurisdiction. Then, suddenly, we find something that is a fair size-after all, something 215 feet long, 45 feet wide and 17 feet deep is not something one tucks underneath an arm. You would think someone would know about it, but apparently somehow it slipped away from the Department of Transport into the Department of Public Works. I think it points up, Mr. Chairman, not only the care with which we have to examine all statements that are made in this house, but the impressions that are left with us and even sometimes the wording of an act.
It points up also some of the inconsistencies in these government operations. Could anything be more foolish, could anything be more senseless, than that the Department of Transport should have jurisdiction over practically all the canals and locks in Canada except two, one out in Manitoba somewhere and the other down in Poupore, Quebec. One can see how this would gradually drift so that eventually the two departments perhaps would each have an interest in the canal. Before we know it we could get into quite a confused situation.

Most of all, Mr. Chairman, it points up the minister's diatribe this afternoon in answer to one of my colleagues who had made a suggestion that was not based on the facts of the case, and then the minister indicated that he was the sole person responsible for canals and locks in Canada. The minister was arguing from facts which were not quite correct, and I have cited my authority for stating that.
Then again, I cast my mind back, Mr. Chairman, to a rather innocent question I asked of the minister a while ago. It appears in Hansard for April 14, 1954, page 4074. The question referred to something called the Wellington street tunnel in the city of Montreal. I remember at the time the chuckles that arose, and the smile on the minister's face, when he good-naturedly and I presume also seriously, pointed out twice in the course of about four sentences how the member for St. Ann had raised the same question previously in the railways and shipping committee. The only trouble was, you see, Mr. Chairman, that despite the fact I had carefully telephoned the minister's office and given him an indication I was going to ask this question, this was another case where somehow the cogs had slipped a little. We were not talking about the same thing, although my question was quite clear. The minister indicated it had been discussed, and something vaguely relating to the subject had been discussed. As a matter of fact, it is rather amusing. The committee evidence at page 110 shows that the member for St. Ann had questioned the replacement of the tunnel on Wellington street between Congregation and Richmond. He said:
This tunnel is over 80 years old.
You mean bridge?
It is a subway.
An overpass.

Yes, that is right.
So, they finally decided it was an overpass. They reached agreement on the overpass. An overpass is something that goes over, Mr. Chairman, it carries traffic over and a tunnel is something that goes underneath.
No.

Well, I think it is necessary to point that out because obviously the minister had missed the import of this particular question. I would point out, just so he can dig back into the facts, that I was talking about what is very commonly known in Montreal, and by the people who deal with it, as the Wellington street tunnel. The Wellington street tunnel is about a half mile removed from the project to which he referred in his answer and it goes underneath the canal. It is a very sizeable operation. 1 would still like, at some point, to get an

answer to my quite legitimate question asked of the minister in this house on April 14, and I hope perhaps without the levity that marked that occasion.
Turning for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to the airports of Canada, may I say that the transportation of passengers by air in Canada has had a tremendous growth in the past 10 to 15 years, as I think all of us know. Perhaps it is well to remind ourselves, however, that in 1941 Trans-Canada Air Lines carried some 103,000 passengers, and in 1952 it carried more than 10 times as many,
1,133,000	passengers. All air lines combined in 1941 carried 181,000 passengers, and in 1951, 10 years later, carried 1,789,000 passengers. Up to now the air transport industry has had a phenomenal record, and with the growth and development of tourist flights as well as the other innovations that are being introduced, we can expect it to grow steadily and rapidly.
Eut, Mr. Chairman, we do not find that adequate facilities exist at the present time to compare with the quick moving steps that are being taken by that industry. Let me make it quite plain, sir, that I am making a difference here between such things as landing strips and equipment of the airport, with which I am not concerned, and the passenger facilities at the airports, with which I am concerned. I have a reasonable acquaintance I think, though perhaps not as extensive as the minister's, with Canada's airports, and they are shamefully inadequate in almost every case. In fact, I think the minister recognizes this because he was quoted in Canadian Aviation magazine, which is a recognized trade paper in the field. In the issue for March of this year-
I do not think, even if the hon. member will quote what I said, that I used the word "shamefacedly", which is the expression he used.

I was coming to your
quotation.

My hon. friend has said that I have already admitted that, as he put it, airport facilities are shamefacedly lacking in Canada. If that is the statement my hon. friend has made, then I am afraid I have to deny it.

Mr. Chairman, there is a terminology in use in radio in which you say, "I did not hear you properly; will you say it again." I think that in this case that is what has happened between the minister and me. I did not use the word "shamefacedly". I said-and I think perhaps the record will show it-that Canada's airports-and these

are my words, this is my interpretation, and as a result of my experience-that Canada's airports are shamefully inadequate in almost every case.
Then I went ahead to say that I felt the minister perhaps recognized this, and then I was going to go ahead and-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. I am not going to allow the hon. member to put words in my mouth, which he has no authority either directly or indirectly to do. If my hon. friend is resorting to a trick, then I am sure this is not the place in which to resort to it. He may use his own words, if he wishes, and he may quote me if he wishes; but he certainly should not leave the innuendo here that I have admitted that airport facilities of this country are shamefacedly lacking-because I make no such admission.
He did not say "shamefacedly"; he said "shamefully."

Order. I do not think there is any necessity for this little interchange to go farther.
