Without attempting in any way to link the quotation I shall now use with my previous opinion-and which I very carefully defined as being expressed as my previous opinion-I shall quote from the March issue of Canadian Aviation in which, as a result of a query, the minister is quoted as saying:
My own extensive experience as a user of air travel has made me acutely aware for some considerable time that our terminal facilities have not kept pace with the growth of air traffic. In offering these comments I should like to make it clear that I am not apologizing for the present situation since those of us who are responsible have done all that the circumstances in the case have permitted us to do.
That is the end of the quotation; and that was the quotation which I intended to use in the beginning. I hope it is satisfactory. Then, let us see what this magazine, one of the standard periodicals in the field, has to say about our present air terminal facilities. It says:
Our air terminals seem to be regarded by those responsible for them in much the same way as our weather is regarded. They do not come up to expectations but willy-nilly we the public should put up with them the best way we can.
While the weather remains largely beyond our control, we believe the present inadequate state of our air terminals could and should be improved. Like the majority of informed public opinion we polled on the question, who describe our terminals as outhouses, barns and stockyards, we think that any change would be an improvement.
And that is the end of that quotation.
Now, we must remember that the attitude of the public toward transportation generally is largely conditioned by what they find at the beginning and the end of their journey. And to the extent that our terminals are inadequate and poor, we are holding back and harming this air transport industry which has done so much for the development of our country.
We do get the impression, from various expressions of opinion and by government figures, that the long-range planning they have under way provides better facilities. Unfortunately, in the long-range we are all going to be dead. And I, for one, am much more interested, as I believe the travelling public of Canada are, in the terminals we can use this year and the next year, and in the immediate future. It will be very nice for those who come after us to have fine terminals, too. But certainly I would like to feel that they are going to be available for us; now, in the next year or two.
It comes down to a charge which I laid at the door of the minister not too long ago, in another debate, a charge of lack of confidence, lack of belief that these things can actually

be happening in Canada, things that justify big thinking, that justify sound planning which will fit in with the type of thing which is happening day after day here in our country.
Let me give the committee the opinion of one of the recognized authorities in air transportation, Sir William Hildred, who was formerly located in Canada in conjunction with the international air transport association, in Montreal. Sir William Hildred says:
II you build an airport small, with due regard to ratepayers' interest, you lose all their money and build a white elephant and not an airport; if you build with due regard to the future and make it a size which you think is about right, you lose half your money and build a grey elephant; but if you make the best estimate you can and multiply it by three and calculate on a size which seems extravagant, you have a reasonable chance of not losing your money, and of not building an elephant at all; but an airport which will serve its time and generation.
Let me say at once that I do not want that word "extravagant" thrown back in my face in the course of the next few moments, because I am not counselling extravagance. I am counselling a realistic realization of what is happening in air passenger traffic in Canada today, and suggesting that we must build in accordance with that.
Just in case the minister would be interested in the comments of one or two of the travelling public on this question of airports, the comments of people who are quite conversant with airports generally, I turn to the February issue of this same publication, Canadian Aviation, because it has made an exhaustive study of the subject. Mr. G. W. G. McConachie, president of Canadian Pacific Air Lines, says this in part:
The passenger-handling facilities, on the other hand, will require major improvement if air travellers in this country are to receive the high standard of service on the ground that they have come to expect in flight.
John Fisher, the C.B.C. commentator, has quite a lengthy and a burning commentary on our airport facilities. I shall just quote this:
They are the most unimaginative and uncomfortable facilities I have found in any civilized country. We simply cannot hold a candle to Europe and most places in the United States. Even Hutchinson, Kansas, has a better terminal than Toronto, Ontario.
He continues:
It is unfair to have the good name of T.C.A. and C.P.A. linked with such poor service. Unfortunately they get the blame for these shortcomings. I think both carriers should have more say in the original planning of these terminal facilities.
Another man who is perhaps well-known here in Ottawa is Mr. Austin Cross, the Citizen writer. He says in part:
As to our air service, it is excellent, dependable, and safe as your Aunt Emma.

It is only when you land you think you are in Lower Slobbovia and not in Canada.
My final quotation will be from a well-known public man, Mr. Joseph M. Pigott, president of the Pigott Construction Company Limited. He says:
Our airport facilities to my mind have always been planned without regard to the expansion and service that was going on. It has been my observation in a great number of cases that, just as the construction of an airport is nearing completion, a start is made to expand and enlarge it.
I could go on with these quotations but I do not intend to. There are many; they all pay tribute to the facilities for handling the aircraft in the air, the safety facilities, and things like that. We may have seen isolated cases in the past where the government has been at fault in respect to regulations, but I do not want to misinterpret the article here or the opinions of many of these people. Many of them are prepared to accept as reasonably adequate or better than adequate what happens when the aircraft leaves the ground, but almost without exception they make burning comments about the quality of the buildings and the facilities that are available to handle passenger traffic.
I have a few little examples from my own experience in this country. There is what you might call class distinction in the toilets at Dorval airport, and I understand this exists in other places. Where else but in a government office would you find three such utilitarian objects set up side by side, one of which is free, the next one where, for the payment of a nickel, you get the same facilities and the next, for the payment of a dime, you get something which is sterilized and heated with ultraviolet ray lights? Really, I could not believe it, Mr. Chairman, when somebody brought this to my attention. I had to wait until a few days after when I was at the airport, and I went in and checked it myself. I could not believe that the government would be doing anything quite as senseless as that. That is the sort of thing which is going on in our airports. If that is the sort of thing that is going on in our air terminals I can easily understand why they are not as adequate as they might be.
Then of course we have the airport out here at Uplands which is familiar to us all. What an amazing building it is to be located in the capital of one of the world's great countries. Frankly, it is little better than a shack. There are no restaurant facilities. In one corner there is a cooler, and if you put a coin in it you get a bottle of Coca-Cola or some other soft drink. On the other side of the room there is another cooler, and if you put a coin in it you will get a cup of
Supply-Transport
coffee, and that is all. Those are the restaurant facilities in the air terminal of Canada's capital. Your baggage is slung across a counter. It is attended to by the personnel, but they have very little facilities for handling it. You are crowded into a room which is so limited in capacity that it is seldom, when you are going out and coming in, that everybody can find a seat at once. To my mind, Mr. Chairman, it is a damning indictment of the entire operation of the Department of Transport in so far as air terminal facilities are concerned across this country, because it is not an isolated case. It is not the sort of thing that just happens, but it does happen in varying degree, some a little bit better, and some a little bit worse, right across this country in airport after airport. If anyone doubts my word I suggest that they take the time to go out on an inspection tour of the air terminals.
I doubt your word very seriously.
May I suggest you make an inspection?
I have made an inspection. I do not think you are competent to deal with this matter.

I am delighted to hear the minister say that because I am one lone person, sir. I doubt very much whether, from the many facilities which you have at hand and the millions of dollars that you are spending on these airports, along with the people that you have at your disposal to think these things through for you and to plan and to see that these can be done, you are justified in making a remark like that, sir.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, not only do I make that remark, I say that your speech is one of sour grapes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I suggest you address the Chair.
On a point of order, the minister should not interrupt an hon. member who is speaking, and having interrupted he should not make the statement he did. He should withdraw.
I have no intention of withdrawing the statement. The hon. member raised his voice in such a way that he prompted the interruption that I made.
The minister should address the Chair.

I agree with the Leader of the Opposition, and the hon. member should address the Chair, also.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I do not consider that the expression "sour grapes" can be regarded as unparliamentary; but I would remind tooth hon. members who have apparently held the floor in the last two minutes that the debate will be carried on better if both of them were to obey the standing practice and address the Chair.
It being six o'clock I do now leave the Chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when we rose at six o'clock there was a short intermission for a discussion which did not bear perhaps directly on the subject I was dealing with. We were outlining the present state of Canada's airports and certainly, in so far as the public is concerned, they are in a sorry state. I think, just to finish the discussion, I might add that in Montreal, for example, one has to leave the main building on a rainy day and go across an open space in order to pick up baggage which is of course inconvenient to those who are using the airport. Many of our airports lack adequate porter facilities and many, many of them lack other niceties. I question whether I have ever been in an airport that really had adequate seating accommodation for people who are using it from day to day.
Now, from the various quotations and expressions from various people I have tried to show that there is general agreement on the inadequacy of these facilities at most of our major airports. I am not quite sure what the minister meant when, in an interjection at one point, he said "sour grapes", but I do know that Montreal is perhaps fortunate in the present plans for the airport. I am glad at least that the plans are under way and we understand that within this year construction will commence on something that will begin to approach and perhaps to arrive at the type of facilities required. But I think we should remind the government that just as one swallow does not make a summer, one airport does not make a system, and that we have got to give consideration to this situation right across Canada.
I am not one who feels that just as long as we are satisfied within our own constituency that all is going well. That is a narrow point of view and I think that those of us who are here try to look at this thing from a broad national angle. We realize that these facilities are definitely needed in many, many parts of Canada.

Leaving the question of terminal facilities aside for the moment we might just remind the Minister of Transport, because it does come within his department, that low-flying aircraft are a continuing problem in the part of the country from which I come, and I would like to express my hope, and I go no further than that, that he will ask his officials and his department to make every attempt to control that and eliminate it wherever possible. I would think that many of the commercial air lines particularly who now route themselves straight across certain cities could be persuaded to fly around them coming into the airport, because of the danger inherent in any aeroplane flying over a large concentration of people.
Then, I would like to mention one other thing which I do not think the minister has heard referred to in this house for some time, perhaps not for ten or fifteen years because most of the people who came from my area have sat behind the minister over that period instead of facing him. I refer to the need for adequate fire-boats in the Montreal area. Hon. members will recall that it was only a few months after the fire-boats were supplied in Vancouver and provided with modern and up-to-date equipment that the city was saved from what might have been one of the most disastrous fires of all time on the Vancouver waterfront. It was bad enough, but it was not as bad as it might have been.
In Montreal they have very limited facilities and lack even one really modern adequate up-to-date piece of equipment with which to protect that great port, and I think it would be most unfortunate if anything should ever happen. I would not want the minister to look back and say, "I wish I had put that fire-boat in Montreal." I would much rather be prepared to have the minister supply the required protection in the port and then come back to me in five or ten years time from now and say, "Well, you did not really need it." Fortunately with many of these things we do not know whether we are going to need them or not, but we do have to protect our investment and we have to constantly bear in mind, particularly in these uncertain times, the great value of really adequate waterfront fire protection in the city of Montreal.
Just to recapitulate for a moment, I think we have shown first of all that there is a little uncertainty as to just how many canals are controlled by the minister. We have asked him for an answer on this and I have no doubt one will be forthcoming, arising out of a question asked well over a month ago.
We have outlined some of the inadequacies of the air terminal situation. And here let

me emphasize again, Mr. Chairman, that much of the material from which I quoted was not my own. The minister chose to say I was not qualified to deal with it. I did not take umbrage at that and question whether it was parliamentary or unparliamentary. I might have taken umbrage but I did not, and I quoted from authorities who are quite independent. It is not a question of sour grapes or someone who is unqualified. I suggest that Sir William Hildred, Grant McConachie, president of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and a man like Austin Cross, who has travelled this country and who has been in and out of all these airports, should know what is happening. They represent various points of view. The government expert in the case of Sir William Hildred, the point of view of the operator in a man like Grant McConachie, and the point of view of the ordinary travelling citizen in the case of Mr. Cross. Then, of course, there is the case of Mr. Pigott. These comments, and there are many others in the material I had, are, and I think I used the phrase before, a damning indictment of what this government proposes to foist off on the people of Canada at the present time as adequate airport facilities. Finally, I have drawn attention very briefly to one or two things such as the need of adequate fire protection in Montreal harbour and waterfront, and also the possibility of giving careful consideration to the problem of low-flying aircraft.
Just as I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I do hope that the things I have tried to point out to the minister tonight will not meet with quite the cool reception which was evident about half-way through my speech, because he has a great responsibility to some million and a half people who travel this country on his railroad, through his airports, and along his canals, and they are looking to him to do the best job he can, perhaps even a better job than he is doing now, and to take heed of their complaints and observations.

Mr. Chairman, normally I would not rise in my place to reply to an hon. member in the middle of my estimates because, like any other minister, I am anxious to have them considered with all dispatch. However, I cannot sit here in my seat and allow the hon. member who has just taken his seat to get away in this chamber with the inaccuracies, the exaggerations, the misstatements and the unethical practice in which he has indulged.
Supply-Transport
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I submit to you that the last two statements made by the minister are unparliamentary and should be withdrawn.
Oh, no.

If the minister cannot take
criticism in a better spirit than he is showing right now, there is something wrong.
Where?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What were the two words to which the hon. member takes objection?
Unethical,-
Unethical, inaccurate, exaggerated.
No, Mr. Chairman. The minister said that they were misstatements-which statement is unparliamentary-and also that they were unethical. Both of those statements should be withdrawn.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to be allowed the opportunity to show where the statements are, first of all, inaccurate, exaggerated and unethical.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On previous occasions certain phrases have been declared to be unparliamentary either by a chairman presiding over the committee or a Speaker presiding over the house. I have not before me a complete list of those phrases but I have read them from time to time, and my recollection does not convince me that either of the words to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra refers have been declared to be unparliamentary. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra could draw my attention to a citation which would support his point of order. However, my own recollection is that these two words have not been declared to be unparliamentary.

The statement by the minister that the hon. member had made a misstatement was, in effect, saying that he had told a lie. Therefore it should be withdrawn. To accuse an hon. member of making unethical statements means that he is not speaking as a member of parliament should, and is a reflection on him.
Oh, oh.
I do not intend to be howled down, no matter how many government supporters may feel like doing it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I assure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that he will not be howled down. But I also am afraid that he is not on sound ground when he says

Supply-Transport
that to say an hon. member made a misstatement is equivalent to saying that a member is lying. If any such suggestion were made that the hon. member were lying, I would of course have to call that suggestion unparliamentary. But the words to which the hon. member has taken exception I do not think are words that I can call unparliamentary.
Is Your Honour ruling that a member may rise in his place, accuse another hon. member of making a misstatement and not have to withdraw that accusation?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister, I think, has used the word "misstatement". He has said that he is prepared to go on and elaborate on the misstatement. I do not think that is equivalent to saying that the hon. member who previously had the floor is lying, to use the words used by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra. I do not think it is any reflection on an hon. member if in the course of a speech a mistake is made. I certainly think the minister has a right to show whether a mistake has been made or not. I cannot see that there is anything unparliamentary in that.
Mr. Chairman,-
Oh, oh.

I do not intend to be howled down if I have to stand here for an hour. There is quite a big difference between a mistake and a misstatement. The minister accused the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace of making a misstatement. He did not say that he had made a mistake. There is a great difference, because there is a difference in intent. I submit to Your Honour that the minister should withdraw that charge that the hon. member has made a misstatement. As the minister used the expression, one could only take the meaning that he was charging the hon. member with doing it deliberately. I submit to Your Honour that that charge should be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am totally unable to take from the word "misstatement" the implication the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is apparently taking. A misstatement could be anything from a mistake to something much broader. I cannot possibly call "misstatement", with no amplification whatsoever, out of order. I am afraid that I cannot do it.

If I may be allowed to proceed, Mr. Chairman, I should now like to deal with some of the inaccuracies of the hon. member in his remarks. In his statement earlier this evening he referred to the
[The Chairman.]
deft way in which the minister made it quite obvious that he and his department control the canals of Canada. A little bit later he said: I had a little premonition that perhaps that statement was not technically and completely correct. Still further he went on to say this: Then the minister indicated that he was the sole person responsible for canals and locks in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the hon. member who made those statements to read Hansard and to see whether, at any place, I made any statement akin to that. I deny having made such statements. During the recess I read Hansard twice and nowhere in Hansard-nor did I correct it-could I find any place where I said that I was responsible for the control of canals in Canada or that it was quite obvious that my department controlled all the canals in Canada. I therefore say that I did not make that statement. To that extent my hon. friend was inaccurate in the statement which he made.
Mr. Chairman-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Will the minister permit a question?
No, no. I should like to get on. I have waited ten minutes now.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. As to the quotations which the minister is using from my speech, I was under the impression that Hansard was not available officially for such use until the following day. I am wondering whether the minister took down the material that he is using.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What is the question of
privilege there?
No. I did not take the notes. I have the actual words which were uttered by my hon. friend.
Mr. Chairman-
Sit down.
-that was my point. Is the minister entitled to abstract material from Hansard before it has been made available to the remaining members of the house? Nobody brought me a copy of Hansard.

I want to deal with the second inaccuracy in the remarks which my hon. friend made, when he took me to task for the answer which I gave to him on the orders of the day in answer to a question

concerning the Wellington street tunnel in Montreal. On that occasion he said this:
The only trouble was, you see, Mr. Chairman, that despite the fact I had carefully telephoned the minister's office and given him an indication I was going to ask this question . . .
It is true that he telephoned the minister's office five minutes before 2.30 o'clock indicating that he intended to ask the question. The hon. member says that he gave me an indication. The hon. member knows that when he wishes to ask a question in the house the usual procedure is to give notice. The notice may well be oral but if oral notice is given five or ten minutes before the house opens he cannot usually expect to get a complete answer. But in this case he did get a complete answer because it so happened that the hon. member for St. Ann had been dealing with this very matter, although my hon. friend thinks not. He then gets up in the house and says that I refused to answer the second part of his question. Furthermore, he expects and insists that I answer it at a later date. Let us see if I did answer it on the orders of the day. I refer to page 4074 of Hansard of April 14, 1954 where I find the following:

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Transport. Has he knowledge of any plan for federal aid to improve the Wellington street tunnel in Montreal, or consideration of a new tunnel in its place in the near future?
This was my answer:
All I can say is that during the sittings of the railways and shipping committee, when Mr. Donald Gordon was under examination, the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Healy) raised the same question. After some discussion during the course of the proceedings the president of the Canadian National Railways undertook to give the matter consideration. I understand since that, because of the representations made by the hon. member for St. Ann, the chief engineer of the Canadian National Railways and one of the representatives of the city of Montreal have been in consultation about the matter.
Then follows the answer to the hon. member's question:
With reference to the second part of the hon. member's question, as to the tunnel, I would say that the federal government has already provided, in co-operation with the city of Montreal, two tunnels under the Lachine canal, one at St. Remi street and the other at Atwater street, the first at a cost of about $5 million and the second at a cost of about $7 million. I have no information as to any additional tunnels being provided at this time.
That is the second inaccuracy in my hon. friend's statement. The greatest farce, if I may use the expression, about my hon. friend's speech was the attack which he made on the airports of Canada, his unfairness to me in not quoting fully the letter which I sent
Supply-Transport
to the Canadian Aviation magazine and in not quoting a number of other things which I propose to indicate as I go along. My hon. friend used expressions like this:
... we do not find that adequate facilities exist at the present time to compare with the quick moving steps that are being taken by that industry.
Then he said that Canada's airports are shamefully inadequate in almost every case. Again he repeated that Canada's airports are shamefully inadequate in almost every case. Then, to use his own expression, he said a little later that the condition of Canada's airports is such that it is a damning indictment of the Department of Transport across the country. My hon. friend is free to make that statement, and any hon. member is free to make that statement, but what are the facts? The facts are that that is not the position. The facts are that the airports of Canada are as good as any other country. The airport facilities of Canada compare favourably with those of the United States having regard to the population of our country.
I come now to what I think is the unethical part of my hon. friend's attitude.
He does not mind about that.

He quoted from a letter which I wrote to Mr. Willmot who is the editor of the magazine, Canadian Aviation. I should like to read the words that my hon. friend quoted from that letter. They were these:
My own extensive experience as a user of air travel has made me acutely aware for some considerable time that our terminal facilities have not kept pace with the growth of air traffic. In offering these comments I should like to make it clear that I am not apologizing for the present situation since those of us who are responsible have done all that the circumstances in the case have permitted us to do.
Then my hon. friend said, "That is the end of the quotation; and that was the quotation which I intended to use." But that is not the end of the quotation, Mr. Chairman. The letter goes on and explains the position as it is today. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that no hon. member has the right to rise in his place in this house and say that that is the end of a quotation he is using when in fact it is not the end. I will put on record now the remainder of the quotation which my hon. friend forgot to put on Hansard.
Forgot?

It reads as follows:
These circumstances, however, may be of interest to you and your readers, and I should like to place them before you.

Supply-Transport
There follows the position with reference to air facilities in our country today. I do not want to read the letter but I will deal with air facilities in Canada as I understand them to be and, as I stated earlier, they are excellent. I state now that our airports are in excellent condition. We have one of the finest systems of airports in the world considering our size and population. I say this to my hon. friend, that when one deals with the question of airports there are not only the air terminal buildings, as he seemed to indicate in the latter part of his remarks, but there are the runways, the taxiways, the lighting systems, the meteorological facilities, the radio facilities, and last but not least, the terminal buildings.
It is impossible to have adequate airport facilities in any country unless you start from the bottom, and that is what we did after planning very carefully. We started by building airstrips, and we have two long, strong runways at each of the major airports in Canada, at Gander, Dorval, Malton, Winnipeg and Vancouver. Furthermore, we have established lighting and meteorological facilities since the end of the war in the amount of almost $100 million, so that we have not neglected these facilities in the way that my hon. friend indicates. But my hon. friend seemed to express the same view in his speech that he expressed in an earlier speech and an earlier debate when he said that the Canadian National Railways lacks confidence in this country and that the government lacks confidence in the country. Let me say to him that his speech the other day and his speech today were the most pessimistic speeches I have ever heard in this house. That is why I think I properly termed it "sour grapes".
In the remarks my hon. friend made he was very careful not to quote a number of statements that were made outlining the position of Canada's airport facilities as they are today. Does my hon. friend realize that we in this country, because of the size of Canada, not only have five or six but perhaps ten major airports, that we have ten secondary airports and perhaps 105 or 110 other airports, whereas in the United Kingdom there are not the same number of major airports as we have in Canada? The same can be said of continental Europe. We are in the unfortunate position because of the size of this country that we must have major airports in far greater number than any other country such as those that I have mentioned.
My hon. friend also quoted Sir William Hildred. I thought it was an excellent quotation and I need not repeat it here. But what Sir William Hildred said in the quotation my

hon. friend gave is exactly what we are doing in the Department of Transport. I can say this, that in my conversations with Sir William Hildred, he had indicated to me that he believes that we have been farsighted in planning airport sites in Canada. My hon. friend, in quoting from the February issue of Canadian Aviation magazine, quoted three or perhaps four statements made by certain people in the field of aviation, but he omitted or thought wise not to quote several other statements in the same magazine which were favourable to the position of the Department of Transport.
Let me quote what Mr. English says. He is vice-president of Trans-Canada Air Lines, that is the air line which uses the facilities of the Department of Transport far more than anybody else does. He says this:
And who works for you.
No, he does not work for me. He works for Trans-Canada Air Lines, and that is not under the Department of Transport.
Wrong again.

I quote:
We feel that within the limits of the money it has had to spend, the Department of Transport has done an excellent job in providing the travelling public with the basic requirements for a safe aeronautical operation. Since the war they have expended their annual budget, which is not large, with emphasis on runways, navigational aids both en route and at terminals, and items of that nature. In our opinion this was the correct approach.
Then, I quote from a statement made by Earle Birney, a Canadian writer and professor of English at the University of British Columbia. He had this to say:
On the credit side I'd say Canadian air terminals are clean, with good facilities for telephones, telegraphs, enquiry; washrooms good; well heated and ventilated. Passenger handling, baggage, etc., seems fast, courteous, efficient.
Then I quote from a statement made by a British air line executive, as follows:
In point of fact, I have always been very impressed with the Canadian airports that I have visited in such places as Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver. It appears to me that not only has a great deal of thought gone into their planning, but that by and large there is an excellent mental attitude of flexibility which permits modifications to the facilities as and when they become necessary.
My own personal view is that this is a proper approach. It is frequently possible to plan for the optimum, but it would be unwise, from a financial point of view to create immediately facilities far beyond the actual and immediate anticipated needs. It is important, in my opinion, so to plan the facilities that they can be increased, modified or amended as the requirements become known.
There are four other quotations that I could give from that issue and the following

issue of Canadian Aviation, which my hon. friend could have read, but he put on Hansard the worst possible position in so far as the facilities of the department are concerned. He thus helped to create an impression which I say with the greatest of deference is not in accordance with the facts. I repeat that we in the Department of Transport have had in mind a program of development for our airports. First of all, we had to begin with the facilities that were most important. We did not begin to build air terminal buildings before the business developed, before the air lines could bring in the passengers. We kept that for the last phase of development.
Most of these facilities were built, established and approved by this house when my hon. friend was not a member of this house. I do not say that to him with any degree of reproach, but I ask him to look at some of the things that have been done in the past by the department, in co-operation with other departments. If he had done so, I am sure he would not have made some of the statements that he made this afternoon. With these estimates we are now beginning a program of expansion of air terminals. We have already built two air terminal buildings, one at Moncton and one at the lakehead. I would invite my hon. friend, and any other hon. member in this house, to go to Moncton and the lakehead and see for himself the kind of air terminal building both of these are. Having regard to the population in the areas, they are excellent facilities and compare with similar airports in the United States of which there are a far greater number of people using the air lines than in either the lakehead or Moncton.
We are proceeding to build two other terminal facilities at the moment, one at Gander and one at Saskatoon. They are being built this year. Of course, as my hon. friend says, at Dorval in the city of Montreal we propose building what we expect will be a large terminal building. There are other places in Canada which I need not mention at this time because I have not the time at my disposal at which we propose to proceed with the construction of air terminal buildings. I say that my hon. friend should have a little more confidence in the desire of these employees, these public servants in the Department of Transport who are as anxious as he is to see to it that adequate facilities are provided for the travelling public.
Let me add this. I think that my hon. friend, in his statement of lack of confidence, is also inaccurate and exaggerated, because I do not think that any organization has shown greater confidence in the future of Canada than has the air transport board, the air
Supply-Transport
services branch, and the Canadian National Railways of which my hon. friend was highly critical. I believe no institution has shown greater confidence in Canada in the building of the many lines which it has built, than has the Canadian National Railways. I know the house is not satisfied with the number of lines built and would like to see far more, but so would I and so would the Canadian National. Under all the circumstances, the Canadian National Railways must work with the funds that are available to them.
Lastly, my hon. friend raised the question of a fire boat for the city of Montreal. As I understand my hon. friend is an alderman in the city council, I am sure he knows that fire protection and the like are matters which fall under the jurisdiction of municipalities. The city of Montreal has made representations from time to time, and knows what the position of the federal government is. The position has always been that fire protection is a matter for the municipality, and not for the federal government. There were exceptions during the war that were removed as soon as the war was over. There is one exception in the case of Vancouver, where a subsidy is paid to the city but the ship was furnished at the sole expense of the city of Vancouver. On all occasions I have clearly indicated in this house and elsewhere that if the city of Montreal or any other national harbour wishes to do the same thing as the city of Vancouver, their application will be considered in the same way.
Now my hon. friend also condemns the facilities at Uplands. I doubt that he should have made the statements which he has, because if he had been here the last years he would have seen how the house approved the tremendous expenditure for runways at Uplands. There will be at Uplands, I think, the longest and the strongest runways perhaps of any airport in Canada, and that for specific reasons. We have I.L.S. facilities there; we have established full traffic control facilities such as at Gander and we have the best meteorological facilities. These facilities cost a tremendous amount of money. We have not been able to build air terminal buildings at Uplands thus far, but we will. We will have a small item in the estimates, either later supplementary estimates or next year's main estimates for a terminal building at Uplands.
As I said, planning must begin from the bottom up, and we must wait until we have other facilities before we can go to the fancier and better type of air terminal building. Mr. Chairman, that is all I have to say. I think I have established that many
