of the statements which were made by the hon. member would not have been made3 had he known the facts.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with a matter now which I have raised before. It has been brought to the attention of the minister on previous occasions. I refer to the Canadian National Railways line leading out of Edmonton and going east as far as a point called Heinsburg. Heinsburg is west of the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary, and is only 39 miles away from another point which would complete this line-this point is called Frenchman Butte. For some reason or other-and I still do not know what it is-this line has not been completed. As I said a while ago, I have brought this matter to the attention of the minister before. In 1950 when I did so he gave me a very encouraging reply. He said at that time that the Canadian National Railways officials had this proposed project very high on their list.
Now I do not know what has happened since that time; but I would like to point out to the minister that this particular line is one of the most densely populated farming areas in western Canada. It is also running through an important oil sector known as the Redwater field, one of the biggest oil sectors in western Canada. Then there are other new developments by way of natural gas, and other developments in the oil industry. There is also a salt mine along this particular road.
I would like to know just what the position is today. First of all, why has this matter been left in abeyance until this time? Is there any possibility of this project being dealt with some time in the near future?

May I say to my hon. friend that w'hat I told him earlier was the position at the time I did indicate it to him. The Heinsburg-Frenchman Butte line is one which has been under discussion in this house for many years by a number of hon. members, including the hon. member for Athabaska, some of the members in the C.C.F. group, and of course the hon. member for Vegreville. They have brought it to the attention of the government.
The position taken by the Canadian National Railways has always been that until there is a sufficient amount of traffic available to make the line profitable, it was not justified in recommending the construction of it to the government. At the time I spoke to the hon. member there was some question as to a mine-I do not know whether it was a salt mine or a mill-that was to be established in the area. I do not think that

finally came to fruition. Because of that the Canadian National Railways have not recommended in recent years the construction of that line. However, in view of what my hon. friend has said I will ask them to review the position again, and ascertain if there is any change.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the minister has had occasion to be a bit out of sorts this evening I would like to preface my remarks by thanking him for something, namely the new additions to the old C.N.R. station at Woodstock, Ontario, although I must confess I was not exactly pleased by the manner in which this news was communicated to the riding.
However, before I get around to that I should like to deal first of all with this matter of the Canadian merchant navy, which has been dealt with already by several other hon. members in the debate. At the outset let me say that I fully agree with the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert with regard to the merchant navy, and as to why at all costs Canada should retain her merchant fleet.
The merchant marine of this country is every bit as essential an arm of our defence forces as are the army, the air force and the navy; and I think it is a very dangerous thing for any government to take a chance on gambling on the security of the country, when it comes to a small subsidy of $100,000 for a ship which, I understand, would amount to a total of about $3 million.
In the hope that I may not be accused of making inaccurate or wild statements, I should like to point out something which I think will back up my argument that the merchant navy is as important in its own way as the other fighting forces of Canada. First of all, let us take the example we have often heard. We have heard it said that Canada does not need a merchant navy because if there is a war we could send our goods to those points in the world they may have to go by using ships of the United Kingdom, the United States or others of our allies. That, of course, is very true. But the same argument might apply to our regular navy, that we can be well defended by the ships of the United States and of the United Kingdom. And if the argument is carried to its extreme it could be used in connection with the air force and the army.
I am sure no hon. member would agree with that argument. But if we are to take the argument to its logical conclusion, that is where it would lead. I feel Canada should do its share to maintain its merchant navy, or its share of the merchant fleet of the allied

countries. Let us see for example what might happen if we do not have a merchant navy of our own. It might very well occur that Canadian materials of war would have to be shipped to some countries in, let us say, South America, during the term of the so-called cold war. It might be that, for reasons of international policy, ships of the United States or the United Kingdom might not wish to carry those arms. How could we get them there?
Perhaps that is a hypothetical example, but it illustrates the point I make. Let us also suppose that there might be a sudden invasion of the northern part of Canada, and that we might be required to get supplies and equipment up there. With no merchant ships of our own, it might be that our neighbour to the south would not have any ships available.
That is an example of what could happen, and for these reasons I say it is dangerous to be without a merchant marine. Then, a further point is that in the event of a world war, Canadian harbour, dock and repair facilities would be a little farther out of the reach of potential enemy bombers than are the great cities of Europe or, for that matter, the large centres of the United States. If we let our merchant marine go completely, it would mean that dockyard workers would be out of practice in repairing ships. Our repair facilities probably would be transferred to some other type of industry. These facts, in themselves, are dangerous.
Perhaps the most important reason of all from the point of view of defence for retaining the merchant marine is the question of what is likely to happen if there is another war. If war should break out-and I am referring of course to a general world war- undoubtedly it would come with unexpected swiftness, and might very well be decided in a few days. Undoubtedly the large ports of England, the continent and the United States would be hit by nuclear weapons; atomic or hydrogen bombs, or future refinements of the same thing. With the possible exceptions of Vancouver, Halifax and Montreal, most Canadian ports would not likely be the targets for those atomic or hydrogen bombs. And, with all due respect to Halifax and Vancouver, I doubt very much whether even they would be thus attacked. Montreal would be the only imminent possibility, or probability. The same could not be said of San Francisco, New York, Boston or Philadelphia.
It is very likely that in these great world ports a large amount of the merchant shipping which would be available to the allies would be knocked out of commission right off the bat. If Canada keeps a merchant
Supply-Transport
marine, even though it is a small one, there is a reasonable chance that a certain proportion of it at some time or other would also be in Canadian ports. Those few ships of ours, even though they might form a very small percentage of the merchant pool of shipping, might prove to be the saving factor in a future world war, because we would have them and our larger allies, the United States and the United Kingdom, might be temporarily incapacitated by a sudden and unexpected attack. Because of the new type of warfare that may be carried on I feel that even a few extra ships at Saint John, Halifax, Quebec and St. John's, Newfoundland might form the saving grace at some future time.
Another matter to which I should like to refer is that of training personnel. Unlike at the time of the second world war when Canada had a very small permanent navy to start with-we had to rely to a very great extent at that time on former merchant service people to help man the ships which we obtained from the United States or we eventually built ourselves-we have a large number of ex-naval personnel who are civilians in active or inactive reserves. We have a much larger permanent navy, but nevertheless a lot of people who are in the naval reserve, active or inactive, have been away from the ships a long time. In addition to that, some people who have recently joined the permanent navy have not had too much experience of seamanship and navigation. I should like to remind hon. members who have never been in the navy that you cannot learn seamanship or navigation overnight or out of a textbook. You have to get that by experience. In the event of war breaking out the navy will require tugs, tenders and all that sort of thing, not to mention trained seamen to man new ships or ships pulled out of mothballs here or in the United States. We would require personnel who are competent seamen and competent navigators. They would be the saving factor that they were the last time. For these reasons it is a great mistake, for the matter of $3 million, to sacrifice our merchant navy.
Let me summarize once more the reasons why I think it is necessary to have a pool of trained personnel in the event of an emergency. First of all, there is the fact that the great ports with large numbers of merchant shipping in the United States and the United Kingdom could very well be knocked out of commission at the start of a war which involved nuclear weapons. Any Canadian ships that were lying in Canadian ports would be a safety factor.
Then, there is the fact that it is dangerous to let our shipbuilding facilities go out of

Supply-Transport
commission, which will undoubtedly happen if we let our merchant navy disappear. Lastly, and probably the most important, is the fact that the merchant service is a branch of our armed services, the same as the regular navy, the army and the air force, because in the matter of logistics it requires the merchant navy to keep the supplies of material in position at points A and B. Without a merchant navy we are placing ourselves in a dangerous position and gambling with the safety of our country for a so-called pittance of $3 million, which is a pittance when compared with the rest of the defence estimates.
There are two other items which I should like to deal with very briefly. The first is the matter of the St. Lawrence seaway. I was pleased to observe in the press today that we are going to start building the seaway in two weeks' time. This will be of very great value not only to the riding I represent but to all the ridings in southwestern Ontario. The very fact that small ocean freighters and large lake freighters will be able to move freely along that waterway will make a great deal of difference. For example, limestone, which is found in the township of West Zorra-and I believe it is the highest grade of limestone in North America for smelting purposes-can be moved down the St. Lawrence to Sydney and to the smelting mills which may be built down the St. Lawrence. Large bulky cargoes, such as turnips, tobacco and machinery can be moved by slow water transport along with limestone and be of great assistance to my part of the country. In return, coal can be brought back from Cape Breton and thereby help the hon. member for Cape Breton South to get rid of the coal they have down there, which we hear a lot about. That coal can be brought up to various parts of Ontario where it can be used, although it is soft coal rather than hard.
The last item I should like to mention is again a localized item in my particular riding. I refer to the railway station which I mentioned earlier in my remarks. This station was built 85 years ago, and I am very glad to know that it is to be fixed up. The sum of $35,000 is to be spent on it. I was pleased to see the suggested plans for improving the station, and they look very good to me. One of the particular objections there is not that the station is old and decrepit, so to speak. We could get along with it if there was some better way of getting to it in the city of Woodstock.
I should like to point out to the minister, as I have already done to Mr. Donald Gordon, for the purpose of the record, that the Canadian National railway station at Woodstock is located to the south of the city.

Eighty per cent of the city is to the north of the tracks. The only way of getting to the railway station from the rest of the city is over a very narrow one-way wooden bridge. "One-way" is perhaps not completely accurate. Two automobiles can pass on the bridge, but they will scrape fenders. If you get a truck or a transport or anything of that nature on the bridge it is impossible for more than one vehicle at a time to go over the bridge. This bridge is built in the shape of a large rounded arc. If you start from one side of the bridge you cannot see whether anything is coming up from the other side, and if you meet another vehicle in the middle one of you has to give way, and it is usually not the truck.
As I said, this bridge was built about 85 years ago. In the wintertime it is heavily covered with ice. A traffic problem is created at the bottom of either end of this bridge. There are frequent petty accidents, and it makes it almost impossible to get to the station on time. It too frequently happens that somebody trying to get to the station leaves to get there on time and he gets to one end of the bridge and finds some big transport or truck still on the bridge or coming over and the individual finally arrives just in time to see the train pulling out of the station.
As I say, this bridge which forms the main method of approach to the station, was built many years ago before the age of large transports and motor trucks. To aggravate the situation even further, on the same side of the railway tracks as the station there is a company which manufactures trucks and trailer equipment, and there is a large transport company as well, the vehicles of which go over this bridge all the time, not to mention the regular farmers' trucks and everything else and the other delivery trucks that use the bridge. In addition, one of the largest feed companies in Canada, the Purina Company, has commenced to build six new grain elevators on the south side of the railway tracks, on the same side as the station is located, and more trucks will be going over and the problem will be getting worse instead of better.
All this leads up to one thing. As I said before, we are very grateful to have the station fixed up and to have modern facilities of all kinds there, to have it well lighted and a clean and comfortable waiting room; but if we can get a modern two-way approach to the railway station from the main part of the city we shall be even happier. So that the minister will draw no wrong inferences from my remarks I should say that there are ways of getting from the main part of the

city to the Canadian National Railway station apart from this one-way approach. If you go about ten blocks one way it is possible to cross the tracks, but it is an exceedingly long and roundabout method. At the other end of this railway station there is a narrow wooden bridge of the same vintage as the one I mentioned earlier, but I do not think it has been used at any time. Because the approaches to this other narrow wooden bridge are so difficult to get at no one ever used it and I believe it is narrower than the first one I mentioned. To conclude my remarks on the station I would just like to express the hope that this matter will be referred through the minister to the C.N.R. officials so they can study it at some future date.
Lastly, and before sitting down, I would like to refer to a local railway crossing in the county of Oxford which is quite famous in that part of the country, but famous inasmuch as it collects anywhere from between one and two to several, which is more than two, carloads of people every year. This railway crossing, known as Creditville, crosses No. 2 highway, one of the principal highways in Ontario. This crossing carries the main Canadian National railway line from Montreal to Chicago and one of the principal reasons for the multiplicity of accidents at this Creditville crossing is due to the fact that it is double track. People see the train coming one way and start up before realizing that a train is coming from the other direction concealed by one of the passing trains.
I do not think there is a railway crossing in western Ontario which has had a greater number of accidents than this one. No doubt the minister will be able to check into that. There might be some others which have as many but none I think have more. The terrain there would not be suitable for the construction of an overpass, but it would be very suitable for the construction of an underpass. I do not think it would be very expensive, particularly in view of the fact that it would prevent a great many accidents in future.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to allow this opportunity to pass without expressing the appreciation of the people at the lakehead for the construction of the airport there. We asked for a permanent building about five years ago and we have now got one of the finest in Canada. It was constructed two years ago and the runways are to be extended so that the largest planes in Canada can land there. Those hon. members who expect to make a trip to Vancouver this fall will get an eyeful.
I have just one more thing to say, namely that this is in keeping with Canada's need.
Supply-Transport
The head of the lakes is fast becoming the hub of Canada and with the opening of the St. Lawrence waterways that airfield will be greatly in demand. I have one request though to make of the minister and that is that when the contract in regard to this work is being let he will see to it that local labour is employed and not men from Toronto and Montreal or anywhere else who cannot do half as good a day's work as the men from the head of the lakes.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that we live in an age of rapid transit I am sure the Minister of Transport will not have too much difficulty in moving his mind back and forth from one side of the country to the other, and perhaps rather rapidly on occasions.
I have some matters I would like to draw to his attention particularly when we are discussing this item on his estimates. I have had some matters brought to my attention which represent quite a considerable problem, and while I am coming to realize that the department for which the minister is responsible is a very complicated one-one in which some of the complications arise out of the fact that the technical questions in relation to transport are becoming increasingly complex-and that can to some extent be explained by the fact that his department, perhaps as much as any other, is affected by the current growing pains of the Canadian nation.
I think you will understand that in various parts of this country today various problems arise which affect every one of us specifically. However, on this occasion I will attempt to set these problems before him and the house and then attempt to draw one or two conclusions which I hope he will consider to be of a constructive nature as they affect the solving of these problems.
I think I can do this in no better fashion than by making reference to some of the communications I have received since I became a member of this house, all of which are related directly or indirectly to the question of transportation. I will start by mentioning a typical one which was addressed to me by the secretary of the co-operative at a place known as Owen Bay. The letter reads as follows:
We wish to call to your attention the serious situation arising from the fact that residents of the numerous islands are left without adequate boat service.
That is typical of the sort of letter which I seem to have been receiving in an almost endless chain. Similar letters come to me

Supply-Transport
from such places as Mansons Landing and Seaford; in fact, Mrs. Dowling of Seaford wrote me as follows:
I am taking the liberty of writing you a few lines to see if you could help us to get the boat to stop in at Seaford again.
I feel rather foolish about the boat not calling at Seaford as X made a trip over to the public works department at New Westminster in regard to the float at Seaford.
It appears that the wharf there was eventually repaired but by the time it was repaired the boat in question had decided not to call there any more. She goes on:
We are getting to the point where we don't know whether to laugh, cry or sell our places and head for the city.
My grandfather was one of the first settlers here so, of course, I rather hate to leave if there is any chance of getting things straightened out again.
Then I have another letter from this place which states:
I am dropping you a letter regarding our mail service at Seaford P.O. which is non-existent at the present time.
We trust that you will be able to contact the correct party and have the aforesaid condition corrected.
I assumed that in this instance the correct party would be the Postmaster General and I wrote him and received a very courteous response to my inquiry in regard to this matter. Here is a case where, in effect, I would like to come to the aid of the Postmaster General through the good offices of the Minister of Transport. I think this letter from the Postmaster General dealing with this problem serves to illustrate very well the nature of the problem which I can see developing in the coastal areas of British Columbia. The Postmaster General's letter reads as follows:
At the beginning of February 1953 information was received that the wharf had become unserviceable, and steamer calls were discontinued. It was therefore necessary to discontinue the above mail service. Arrangements were made for a temporary service between Seaford post office and Mansons Landing.
Later the letter continues:
There was some question of whether the Department of Public Works would repair the wharf at Seaford, but eventually they decided to do so. Repairs were completed in December 1953 and it was anticipated that the regular Seaford and wharf mail service, described in the first paragraph, would be resumed.
However, even though the wharf was repaired, the Tidewater Shipping Company advised that they were unwilling to call at Seaford directly-
So that, under the circumstances, he goes on to say that they were not in a position to give that mail service. Then we come to another island, namely Hornby island, where over a period of time they have been attempting to develop some sort of ferry service to replace the steamer service which

is no longer existent so far as that island is concerned. In a communication from the Hornby island people setting forth their problem, we find it described in this fashion: Existing Conditions
1.	A beach landing craft ferry boat is now operating on a daily schedule under a provincial government subsidy of $5,000 per annum. This ferry is now the only means of passenger and freight transportation to and from Hornby island. No other boat service is available or pending.
2.	The ferry is operating at present between Gravelly bay (Denman island) and Phipps point (Hornby island) because the latter is the only point where cars can embark or land at present.
3.	The service is crippled by lack of adequate landings. At no tide lower than 6 feet can cars embark or disembark under any circumstances on either side of the channel.
4.	Tides during the winter are reasonably high during the daytime so that in general service has been maintained, though in a hazardous fashion in rough weather and particularly in snow and ice conditions.
5.	Tides during the summer months are generally low during the daytime and service will be seriously curtailed during the time when it is most needed and particularly during the tourist season from June to September.
6.	There is no protection whatsoever available for the boat when tied up and during stormy weather conditions are extremely hazardous to its safety.
That communication sets forth another aspect of this problem. Then we go up a little bit further north to Quadra island. In a brief drawn up by the Quadra island ratepayers association and endorsed by the Campbell River chamber of commerce some facts in connection with their problems are set forth as follows:
The residents of Quadra island have been attempting to have a car ferry instituted between Campbell River and Quathiaski Cove. Transportation between these points is now served by a small passenger vessel of twenty-four person capacity.
This vessel, which has outgrown its usefulness, is subsidized by the provincial government. The present provincial minister of public works, the Hon. P. A. Gaglardi, recognizes the merits of our necessity for better transportation by agreeing to raise the subsidy to such a level that it will make the operation of a combined car and passenger ferry possible.
However it is his contention that the necessary landing slips are the responsibility of the federal government. The Hon. Mr. Gaglardi points out that the federal government constructed car ferry landing slips in the Gulf islands recently, and suggests there is no reason they shouldn't build them here.
We have recently been in communication with Hon. R. H. Winters, federal Minister of Public Works, requesting that he give favourable consideration to our request. This he has failed to do, contending that the slips are the responsibility of the provincial government and we must look to our local authorities for help.
If the Minister of Public Works were here, I am sure he would agree that the correspondence and the discussions I have had with him confirm that particular statement with regard to the policy of this government.

Then we move across to the far west coast of Vancouver island where Canada really meets the Pacific. I have here a letter from a gentleman by the name of Mr. Rustaud. He discussed the sort of boat service they have on the west coast of the island and asks me to do something about it. In this letter he explained how he has been living on that west coast for the last thirty or forty years and that never in his experience has the boat service been as bad as it is at the present time. Just to show that the Canadian people, wherever they are located, retain some sense of humour, may I say that I have even had suggestions coming from the west coast of the island that they might consider establishing a mule service across the back of Vancouver island. In describing the problem they had, he said that they do not know whether they can provide the right kind of snowshoes for winter service across the mountains or whether they should use mules or donkeys for the purpose.
Then I also have here a letter from the secretary of the Zeballos school district, which is a copy of a letter which he wrote to the department of education in Victoria. Apparently the department had been complaining that the necessary documents of the Zeballos school district were not reaching Victoria within the prescribed time according to the provincial education regulations. He has to reply and explain just what happens in order for them to get their mail, bank vouchers and that sort of thing back and forth. Here is a telegram which I received from Kyuquot and which states:
Our telegram today's date sent forward to Postmaster General Ottawa requesting an immediate extension of air mail services to Kyuquot post office.
This telegram is dated January 3. They say the last mail delivery received was on December 15. Anyone who had been reading the British Columbia papers at that time would recall that a good many of the residents on the west coast of the island did not get their Christmas mail or their Christmas supplies.
Then we come back again to Texada island which is in the gulf. There we find a situation arising out of the fact that the C.P.R. steamer service to Powell River, which had included this island as a port of call, was being withdrawn and that the residents not only of Powell River but of Texada island were not going to have any means whatever of getting their cars in and out of that area. It is perfectly true that plans had been made for the building of a road and the establishment of a car ferry which would 83276-327
Supply-Transport
make car and truck transport to Powell River a possibility. But we find there a situation where a service which has been provided for years is being arbitrarily withdrawn before any substitute is provided to take its place. In the last few years that sort of thing has been happening all over the coastal area. When you follow through correspondence like that which comes consistently from so many places, it seems to me that a sort of pattern begins to emerge. I could, of course, have read a great many more letters than those which I have read, and I could have referred to other places to which I have not referred. Partly because of improved technical facilities and methods of transportation I feel that not only is a revolution taking place in transportation all over Canada but that a particularly difficult one is taking place in an area which relies on a complicated combination of air travel and sea travel and, in some instances, road travel.
It seems to me that a few things emerge out of that picture. In my opinion no one in the house can quarrel with the idea that the purpose of the functioning of the Department of Transport is to assist in meeting the transportation needs of the people of Canada and that if this is not being done then all these millions of dollars or a large part of them are really being spent to no avail.
It seems to me that the correspondence to which I have referred indicates that somehow or other there is a lack of proper co-ordination between the various agencies interested in transportation. It would appear to me that the administration of the various agencies within the Department of Transport, such as the air transport board, the board of transport commissioners and the Canadian maritime commission, is being carried out by very competent people so far as any experience I have had in dealing with them is concerned. However, with respect to an area such as the part of Canada in which I live it would appear that these bodies are not being co-ordinated so that there is an over-all arrangement.
I think further that while the pattern shows that so far as the Department of Transport, the Department of Public Works and the Post Office Department are concerned, each one may be attempting to do a good job within its own sphere. Nevertheless there is no co-ordinated arrangement to see that the most effective type of service is given. I also believe that the car ferry transportation situation to which I have referred indicates that some better form of co-ordination must be devised between the federal transport

Supply-Transport
authorities and the same agencies at the provincial level than exists at the present time. I cannot see that it is necessary, for example, that there should be a runaround on the question of responsibility for a ferry slip here or a ferry slip there, and the people in various communities should not have to resort to the haphazard hit and miss method of appealing first here and then there in order to get action.
Suggestions are being offered in various quarters now that there should be ferry services here and there, but no one seems to accept the responsibility for creating an overall pattern of transportation development. With the technical advances that are being made it would appear to me that that is becoming an increasingly necessary thing to do. As one of the new members of the house I hesitate to attempt to make any detailed analysis of the over-all policy that should be established with regard to such a complicated department as the Department of Transport, but if I may be permitted to make one or two observations I would say that in my opinion there has to be a change in the fundamental concept of the function of the department.
The functions of such bodies as the board of transport commissioners, the air transport board and the Canadian maritime commission are primarily concerned under the present set-up with the question of regulation; they are regulating bodies. It seems to me that if the transportation needs of the country, particularly of the part of Canada which I have been describing, are going to be met the concept of a regulating body has to be changed to that of a planning and co-ordinating body, and that there must be a close liaison between the various forms of transportation.
Some hon. members will recall that for quite a long period of years a subsidy of $100,000 a year, I believe, was paid towards the operation of the famous west coast steamer, the Princess Maquinna. She has now seen the end of her service but while in operation met a need which could have been eliminated almost overnight if certain highways had been built by the provincial government. Without attempting to go too deeply into the question of federal participation in developing a highway system, I believe that in the long run it would be sounder economics if the $100,000 a year which was paid for many years from the federal coffers had been used to assist in the development of a highway system on Vancouver island so that the west coast communities might have had quick and easy access by road to the rest of Canada. We would now have

something to show for the money whereas that subsidy, as indeed in the case of every other subsidy that might be granted, is in effect money down the drain.
I do not know that I expect the minister to accept my thinking with respect to planning transportation entirely, but it seems to me that within certain limitations there has been very effective planning of transportation in Canada. Where some of our able people have been put to work they have produced such services as Trans-Canada Air Lines. The only point I make there is that the planning does not go far enough. It seems to me that if the transportation needs of Canada were regarded as something to be provided for by a national public utility like the Post Office Department it would be possible to plan an over-all transportation system. No one, I think, would quarrel with the idea that it would not be proper if mail service was established from Ottawa to Vancouver and stopped at Vancouver with the result that people living anywhere beyond Vancouver had to get their mail by any sort of hit-or-miss arrangement that they might be able to devise.
In my opinion transportation falls essentially into the same category as the postal service so far as the people of Canada are concerned, and because of the kind of transportation methods being developed I believe the time has come when the only agency in Canada that can accept over-all responsibility for the co-ordination of that service is the federal government. If that responsibility were accepted then provision could be made for the most logical methods of transportation to all communities in Canada, either inland or coastal.
So far as I can see, it would not necessarily mean that some new transportation monopoly would have to be set up. It would mean that there would be responsibility upon someone to see that the most economic transportation services were being provided to all the people, just as the postal authorities accept the responsibility for seeing that the mail is carried by the best possible method. Of course, the mail service, as indicated by some of these letters, is very closely tied to the question of transportation facilities that are available. To that extent, at least we could be killing two birds with one stone.
I would suggest that as a minimum step in this direction consideration should be given to extending the powers of the Canadian maritime commission at least to equal the powers of the air transport board with regard to arranging what facilities are going to be provided, and under what conditions. The arbitrary manner in which various

steamer services are being withdrawn, without any regard as to whether a substitute for them is available, certainly is not creating a satisfactory situation so far as the people in the coastal areas of British Columbia are concerned. When I say that I do not mean that I feel steamer services should have to continue to operate where their operation is completely uneconomic. It should be obvious that with the proper development of the road system, and the use that people are making of cars and trucks, this question of car ferry service is closely tied in with a proper solution of the transportation problem on the coast.
Certainly the passing of responsibility from one level of government to another is not something that should continue. I feel that in mentioning this subject under the estimates of the Minister of Transport I am attempting to point out the fact it is a problem that is beyond the range of policy of only the Department of Public Works or only the Post Office Department. So far as I can see the only department of the federal government that can make a move in the direction of a logical solution is the department for which the Minister of Transport is responsible.

Before we start the consideration of the details of these estimates, I should like to invite the minister's comments on a problem that has not been raised so far this session, that is the problem of the control of that unwelcome by-product of steam transportation, smoke. I shall just take a moment, Mr. Chairman, to indicate to the minister what I have in mind. There have been a good many studies of the control of smoke and air pollution in the major cities. I suggest that it is a matter of concern for the Department of Transport, one of the many concerns of that department, because steam locomotives and steamships are very substantial contributors to air pollution and they are not so directly under the control of the municipalities as industrial plants and other factories, which add to the pollution of the air in our major cities.
I wish to refer to a paper by Professor E. A. Allcut, of the department of mechanical engineering of the University of Toronto which was delivered last year to the American Society of Mechanical Engineers. In this paper he says:
Among the worst offenders with regard to smoke emission are the railroads and steamships, but the municipal authorities have no control over these agencies, as they are under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners for Canada. This is a dominion (federal) board and has the usual characteristics of a governmental department.
Supply-Transport
I am not sure whether that last ambiguous statement is by way of praise or condemnation. He goes on to refer to the problem on the Detroit river where there is a great deal of shipping and transport, and then he comes back to the question of the railways in these words:
The railways also are causing some trouble, particularly in the round-houses. However, they are installing oil lighting-up systems and external steam-starting equipment in several places and are giving special instruction to firemen on proper methods of lighting-up and feeding the fires.
Then, he refers to certain general orders of control and goes on to say that the solution lies largely in the adoption of the diesel locomotive.
Just to give the background of my reason for referring to this matter, Mr. Chairman, the main problem is in the bigger cities. Toronto according to the Ringelmann scale which is used by people who make these studies has an index of smoke density of ten, which is the highest in Canada and is shared by Hamilton, Kingston, Saint John. Montreal, the largest city in Canada, has an index of nine. I should like also to refer to a chart showing the density of pollution in the city of Toronto. This is rather an older chart, 1932, and it indicates that the greatest deposition of smoke material in Toronto is in the vicinity of King and University avenues, just opposite the railway station. At that point the deposit of solids in tons per square mile per year was 645 tons. Going north a half mile to College and University, it is reduced to 453 tons, about two-thirds as much.
The cities have been making substantial efforts to control this problem through bylaws. What I wish to ask the minister to consider is whether there is anything further that can be done under the direction of his department to limit or reduce the pollution in so far as it comes from railway locomotives. I have the figures on dieselization, if I may use that term, on the Canadian National, and the Canadian Pacific has about the same ratio. At the end of last year the steam locomotives numbered 1,804, that is road locomotives, and switching locomotives numbered 498. Then, there were 33 electric locomotives, and I would like to ask the minister where those are employed.
Then we come to the diesels. Of diesel electric road locomotives there were 176; road switching, 101, and diesel switching locomotives, 226. The use of diesels in the larger cities for switching purposes, if practicable, for purposes of taking trains in and out, would make a great contribution to the solution of this difficulty.

Supply-Transport
And it is not an imaginary difficulty. A normal human being takes in 30 pounds of air each day, 2-7 pounds of food and 4-5 pounds of water. We are very careful about the food, and the purity of the water. Notwithstanding the fact, however, that we take in a great deal more air-and some of us seem to give out a great deal of it-we are not so careful about the purity of the air.
While this subject may be considered somewhat remote from a discussion of the estimates, it seemed to me that this was the proper place to raise the issue. I feel some help can be given to the cities. While those cities can inspect locomotives and their fires, to see whether they are being properly fired, they appear to have no control over their operation.
As a final word on the subject may I refer to inspections. Up to July 1 last year, inspectors in Toronto inspected 5,940 industrial plants, 3,787 locomotives and 24 ships, making a total of 9,700 inspections of smoke-emitting fires and furnaces. Inspections disclosed unsatisfactory conditions in 398 plants, 108 locomotives and 22 ships. So that there is a real problem here which may be a proper subject for the minister's attention.

May I take only a moment to deal with this problem, which is indeed a very important and difficult one. I have no doubt the statements made by the hon. member for St. Paul's about the density of smoke in Montreal and Toronto are accurate. The problem has been approached in Montreal-and I shall refer later to Toronto, although I do not know just how it has been dealt with there. But in Montreal the problem was pretty serious and acute, and it was felt that the municipality should do something about it. They made representations to the board of transport commissioners. While the board may not have direct jurisdiction, it does have some control over smoke nuisance. They suggested in the course of the hearing that took place that a committee be established, and this was done by the city of Montreal. It was composed of engineers from that city, as well as representatives from the board of transport commissioners and other groups, such as the board of trade.
I recall that I saw a delegation of about 25 people from Montreal three years ago with respect to this subject. They were then seeking to remove the smoke from the Turcot yard roundhouse. While they did not succeed entirely, their efforts were not in vain because in their anxiety to assist the Canadian National Railways added new equipment which proved to be helpful. While I am not suggesting that the problem in Montreal has been solved-because it has not-the fact is

that it has been attacked in a different fashion. Since that time the railways have decided to dieselize their service.
I know that in Toronto, while there are still some steam locomotives operating in and out of the city, there are far more diesels being operated now than ever before. And with the coming into operation of more and more diesels and switchers the condition will be improved substantially.
The hon. member dealt also with steamships. The board of transport commissioners has no jurisdiction over steamships, certainly not over the smoke emitted from the stacks of steamships. I should think that perhaps if a committee such as the one to which I have already referred has not been established in Toronto, that might be the method of approaching it. I know the railways are anxious to find new technical developments which will assist in doing away with smoke. I can assure my hon. friend that the railways, both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., in co-operation with the board of transport commissioners, are giving the matter serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of taking much time during the debate on the estimates of the Department of Transport.
However, I believe I would be remiss in my duty if I did not inform the house at the proper moment of the opinion not only of the constituents I have the honour of representing but also of all the citizens of Quebec city, on two thorny problems which arouse public opinion at home.
My fellow citizens of Quebec who like their city and have for it a deep attachment are as concerned as anyone else about its progress, development and improvement.
Quebec's greatest industry is undoubtedly the tourist trade which brings every year numerous visitors to the old capital; it has indeed become proverbial and is generally recognized.
Millions of people visit us each year, confident that they will find in Quebec something different, in our way of life, our tradition and our history, as well as in our sites that so eloquently tell of our past.
Referring to the capital city of my province, we always say "Old Quebec". Is it because our city has existed since 1608, when it was founded by Samuel de Champlain, that is, 350 years ago, or is the expression meant to underline conditions which have existed too long already and cannot be improved because of a lack of co-operation?

Both interpretations of the term "Old Quebec" are full of truth, but I prefer the former to the latter, which I endeavoured to reproduce faithfully.
Without further delay, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) will allow me, no doubt, in the name of those I represent, as well as in the name of the people of the city of Quebec in general, to discuss as briefly as possible these two problems which are vital to the development and progress of the city of Quebec, namely to remove level crossings, deepen the St. Charles river and put an end to water pollution in the Lairet river.

(Translation):

It is surely not a new thing for those who live in Quebec to hear about those two problems this subject having been on everybody's lips for the past 25 years and more.
The Quebec municipal council or our chamber of commerce have on occasion been requested to express the whole population's point of view on this matter, so that this problem may be solved with the least possible delay. These two very important and highly representative public bodies have been joined by a great number of organizations of no less importance, social clubs for instance, whose devotion and merits are countless and various citizens' leagues formed in every ward of the old capital city.
All these groups, on several occasions in the last quarter century, and on behalf of all the people of Quebec, have demanded the removal of a number of level crossings situated in two historic constituencies of the capital, namely Quebec East, represented in this house by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and Quebec West, which I have the great honour of representing in the national parliament of the Canadian people.
On September 17, 1953, the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada held hearings in Quebec city. On that occasion Quebec city,

in conjunction with the Quebec chamber of commerce, submitted to the commissioners a brief including a serious and exhaustive study on the removal of the main level crossings in Quebec city.
On February 3, 1954, the representatives of those two influential bodies who had been summoned to Ottawa heard a report and a discussion on the written briefs of the railway companies on the general problem of level crossings across the country. They argued their case in a summary way and promised to produce an additional brief with comments on:
1.	The general principles set forth by the companies.
2.	Their suggestions or recommendations on the general problem and its several aspects, financial, legal and so forth.
3.	The level crossing conditions peculiar to Quebec city.
I do not intend to mention here all the discussions that went on then, but I want to point out the rather strange position taken by the railway companies who wanted the Canadian taxpayers to bear the cost of that grade crossing removal in direct proportion to the benefits they would derive from it.
The companies claim that they should not be called upon to pay for any improvements or systems of protection at grade crossings, when the work is required for the benefit of the users of the road or the public in general, particularly when the railroad has been in existence for a long time. The companies also claim that the road transport companies which compete with them would benefit from, and enjoy all improvements made, without having anything to pay.
In a word, the railway companies warn the general public that if improvements and appropriate protection are deemed necessary, the public should pay for them in the proportion of 90 per cent, while they-the railway companies

would only pay 10 per cent, and this only in the cases that are considered.
The federal government is asked to pay 70 per cent, the provincial and municipal governments not less than 20 per cent.
The federal government can certainly contribute the main part of the amount since it collects from the Canadian taxpayers 77 per cent of the total national revenue. It seems altogether absurd to ask the provinces, which collect only 13 per cent of the taxpayers' money, and the municipalities, who get

barely 10 per cent, to contribute for that purpose. Personally, I think that the federal government and the railroads should bear the whole cost of those improvements.
The grade crossing situation in the city of Quebec is intolerable. Not only does it endanger the lives of the individual citizens but it brings about traffic congestion which is detrimental to the best interests of the city. All day long, numerous passenger and freight trains use the tracks in both directions and very often it seems that the trains are assembled right where the level crossings are situated.
Not only does that fact create a constant risk of death but such interruptions of traffic are prejudicial to the interests of Quebec city. That deplorable situation surely does not encourage the numerous tourists who visit us each year to make, upon their return to their own country, the kind of publicity we would like to have.
Following representations made by the Quebec municipal authorities, the Quebec chamber of commerce and every important organization in the old capital, I would like to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the government to give this serious and urgent problem all the attention it deserves and remedy the situation with the least possible delay. By doing so, the government will enable people from Quebec to add, without hesitation, when asserting that they love their city, that they are also proud of it.
I take this opportunity to submit another request to the Minister of Transport and I am confident that he will gladly support it.
There is only a central station in Quebec city; it is located, as we know, in the eastern part of St. Roch ward. Since the population of Quebec now exceeds 200,000, not counting its floating population, the station has become inadequate for the needs of the large number of people who have to use it. As a result, at certain hours of the day when trains arrive and depart, there is a traffic bottleneck in all the lower part of the city that greatly delays travellers anxious to return home.
I therefore ask for the construction of a new station, which is vitally needed in Quebec, and this station should be located, as everybody agrees, at the foot of St. Sacrement hill, at the limits of the city of Quebec, for the convenience, first of all, of the people of the constituency of Quebec West, and of an important part of the constituency of Quebec South, including the town of Sillery
Supply-Transport
and the municipality of Ste. Foy in the constituency of Quebec-Montmorency. This station would serve a community of no less than 100,000 people.
I lay this request before the minister, and I feel assured that he will take into consideration the interest of the people of the city of Quebec.
The second urgent problem, which I have had the opportunity of mentioning several times already since the beginning of this session, has to do with the deepening of the St. Charles river and the purification of the Lairet river, both of which run through the Prime Minister's constituency.
The St. Charles river, moreover, runs between the riding of Quebec East and the constituency which I have the honour of representing in this house.
For at least 25 years and to a growing extent these two rivers have been little else to the people of Quebec than open air sewers. From them rise nauseating odours that threaten the health of our people. These sickening smells are particularly offensive in the densely populated St. Sauveur and Limoilou districts inhabited by fine, low-salaried working people who, during the summer, have to breathe the foul smells rising from these veritable dumps. These working people are not sufficiently well off to be able to spend the summer in the country and enjoy it as do those who have more money. It would seem that these families, which for the greater part are large, are entitled to some consideration. They should not be forced, during the summer, to breathe these innumerable foul stenches, to say the least, with which these rivers are polluted. The doctors of Quebec all agree in branding these rivers as a source of infection which may well breed contagious diseases, and even epidemics.
I have often heard it said in Quebec city that when there is a flu epidemic or an epidemic of some sort of fever, it is on account of a virus that spreads in the air. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that a more thorough medical investigation would soon show that such a virus-there may be more than one-is to be found only in the St. Charles and Lairet rivers.
I want to assert again that a lot of diseases with which our people are stricken are due to the infectious conditions to be found in these two rivers which are a constant health hazard.
I have already appealed directly to the right hon. Prime Minister in order that those

Supply-Transport
projects which everyone in Quebec is asking for may be started without further delay. Unfortunately I received no answer, and no hope has been given to our good people.
In the dying days of this session I appeal again to the right hon. Prime Minister to provide the solution which every citizen of Quebec is waiting for. The carrying out of such projects would first of all protect the health of our people, it would improve the aspect of Quebec, would free our people from the foul smell of that open air sewage, and would help to solve in Quebec unemployment conditions which are still acute.
People ought to stop telling us that there is no money. The Canadian nation has never been taxed to such an extent since its very beginning, and the federal treasury never was so full.
I do not object to Canada helping foreign nations, and presenting India with $20 million so that it may build a hydro project.
Order.
Order, order.

-but please let us not be so prodigal with the people's money, before our own population benefits from projects that are essential to the protection of its very existence.

the tragedy in which the Chelan was sunk, and all her crew were lost. Here again I must call the attention of the minister to the fact that the only available help came from the United States coastguard service. Because of the position of this wreck, and the position of the nearest unit of the United States coastguard service in Alaskan waters, that help was quite ineffective and so far has not resulted in locating any trace of the wreck or any sign of those who were drowned.
Well may the Vancouver Sun in an editorial of March 16 of this year say "But we need a coastguard". This editorial says:
There is a simple reason why tugboatmen around the port of Vancouver are setting up their own rescue service-they are fed up with Ottawa's repeated "No" to requests for a fully manned, properly equipped B.C. coastguard.
Lives of hundreds of men and millions of dollars' worth of property are at stake on one of the trickiest stretches of coast in the world. "The federal government won't help. We keep seeing valuable lives lost every year", said Capt. Cyril Andrews, of towboat employment agency, who has been the guiding spirit behind the new rescue plan. "So we're linking up with R.C.A.F.'s air-sea rescue organization in a day and night operation. What we're doing is co-ordinating into a set-up the desire of every crewman and officer to help his fellow seamen".
It is roughly calculated that of 318 tugboats located in this area, about 250 are at sea at any given time. This is obviously a handy rescue force available, with the vessels equipped with ship-shore radio or wireless and many with radar. Details of fitting these vessels in with the R.C.A.F. are being arranged.
The plan will be that when R.C.A.F. air-sea rescue watch receives a distress call, in addition to owner, R.C.M.P. and government vessels being alerted as in the past, headauarters of the towboat employment agency will be warned and they will radio tugs at sea in the area.
It is a self-help plan deserving the highest praise. But it is not the complete answer to safety needs on B.C.'s dangerous coast. The Sun repeats again that B.C. must have a coastguard of trained men in fast, seaworthy vessels, one type for use in inland waters, a second for deepsea work.
Ottawa must recognize that it is a national duty to safeguard the lives of seamen and the property they have in their charge.
I noticed the minister was smiling very gaily as I was reading that editorial. I wonder again, as I wondered last year-
On a point of order; I was not smiling at what the hon. member was saying.
All right; I beg your pardon.
I was talking to my officials in front of me, and was listening very carefully to what the hon. member said.

1 am glad to have that assurance from the minister, and to know he realizes this is a very serious problem; that it involves a stretch of coast that

has earned the unenviable name and reputation of being a graveyard of the Pacific. Despite the assurance someone has given the minister that the coast is adequately protected at the present time, the fact remains we are dependent in large measure upon help from the United States coastguard service. In the last few disasters that have taken place, this help has proven inadequate; there has been no effective rescue work performed. These men who are risking their lives every day, because of governmental neglect, are now trying with their inadequate means to protect their own lives through the sort of voluntary organization I have described.
I hope the minister will take this problem and give it serious consideration. I hope he will realize that it is not merely a demand for government help, it is a serious cry for help from men engaged in a most hazardous occupation along probably one of the most dangerous stretches of coast in the whole world.

I am sure my hon. friend will expect me to say something in answer to his observations, and I will say it just as briefly as I can. I am sure he is not aware of what the government has done, otherwise I do not think he would have approached the problem in the manner in which he has. The government has given very careful consideration to this whole question. Some years ago a committee was appointed composed of representatives of the maritime commission, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Fisheries, the Department of National Defence, army, navy, air force, Department of Finance, Department of National Health and Welfare and Department of Transport, to review the arrangements for search and rescue and make recommendations for a more efficient service. That committee considered the subject in detail and there was a debate in the house on the very matter to which my hon. friend now refers. The reference to the committee arose in a similar debate that took place in this house at that time.
I would ask my hon. friend to bear this in mind. The chairman of that committee was none other than a Vancouverite, the then chairman of the Canadian maritime commission, namely Mr. Justice Clyne of the supreme court of British Columbia. He was assigned by the Department of Transport to inquire into the whole question of a coastguard service. In the course of the studies of this committee, this is what they found. To permit Canada to establish an efficient coastguard service there would need to be a capital cost of $9,033,000, and an operational

cost of $2,684,000. A statement made to me by one of the members of this committee indicated that the setting up of a new coastguard service to perform search and rescue duties on the coasts and the great lakes would involve a capital cost of roughly $9 million, would require an annual maintenance additional to the present cost of the R.C.M.P. marine service and the R.C.A.F. search and rescue service, of about $3-25 million, or $12-25 million for such a service.
I do not deny, and neither does the government, that that would be a good thing. The government did not feel it could spend that amount of money because of conclusions of the committee in regard to the cost of establishing a coastguard service at that time. The committee went further and made recommendations which I placed on Hansard at that time, and which are too lengthy to repeat now, but there were a series of recommendations, the object of which was to protect our coasts. One of the main suggestions was that all the departments concerned should review and centralize their activities under one head, and that was the Department of National Defence air service, which would take charge of search and rescue operations on both our coasts.
The same debate took place then as is taking place now; and it was said that we depended on the American coastguard service for safety on our coasts. During that debate the Minister of National Defence placed on the record a number of instances where Canadians went to the rescue of Americans, and pointed out that we did just as much in the way of assistance on the east coast and in the international section of the great lakes for Americans as did Americans for Canadians.
I do not wish to go into this matter in greater detail; but if my hon. friend will look at the debates which took place at that time he will find that there was no intention then, any more than there is today, to neglect the safety of our waters. It was felt that because of the tremendous cost the only thing and the best thing to do was to adopt the recommendations of the committee. But I would not want the hon. member to think that the Department of Transport, through its marine service or any other branch of government, is taking this lightly. On the contrary it is a serious matter, and the day may come when we will have to establish a coastguard service. But because of the many demands which are made not only for this fine service, but for the many others that are raised from time to time, thus far it has been found impossible to meet the wishes of my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, there are just a few further remarks which I think might be made in connection with some I made earlier, in reply to the Minister of Transport. The first thing, of course, that perturbed me-[DOT] perhaps it was a matter of misunderstanding-was that he did not seem to hear clearly some of the remarks I was making. I remember, for example, saying in, I think, a reasonably strong voice, though perhaps not as strong as the minister's, that Canada's airports are shamefully inadequate in almost every case. The minister was very much worried and said, "I do not think that even if the hon. member will quote what I said that I used the word shamefacedly". That is the expression he used. Well, obviously he was not hearing very well.
Then, later on in the same debate I had said that if he does not recognize the airport situation, that is for him to say. And the minister said, "I do not know what my hon. friend is referring to when he speaks of the air force". So perhaps if he had been listening to my remarks that would have helped us along.
Secondly, I was interested to hear him say that his airport and building facilities compared favourably with the United States, having regard to the population. I think perhaps those five little words, "having regard to the population", are an interesting commentary. After all, our population is only 10 per cent of that of the United States; so I presume the minister is happy if he feels that his buildings at our various airports are 10 per cent as good as they are in the United States. Frankly, I do not think that is good enough. And my point is that I definitely cannot accept a statement of this kind, with words such as that hedging it around.
Then the minister attempted to show where he had been misquoted. Well, I was very careful to point out where my quotations started and finished, particularly because the minister had been so worried and we had got into an altercation earlier, even before the quotation was made. And that is why I was so careful to delimit the quotations.
Then of course, in his rebuttal, he missed the point of my argument completely, because I had made a sharp differentiation between landing strips, equipment and buildings. And he, in his reply, went into detail about landing strips, radar and other things which I agree we have. He did not deal adequately with buildings. I tried to be as kind as I could. I did not mention the international airport at Montreal, and I do not propose to mention it now. I imagine however that the minister has some acquaintance with it and knows just what a miserable front door it is for those coming to Canada.

The front door is Gander.

The minister quoted an official of T.C.A. saying how good his airport buildings were. Well, 1 am not too concerned with whether T.C.A. responds to the Minister of Transport or responds to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have a suspicion that if they do-as they do-respond to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, they jump through the hoops even more readily, and they would be even more inclined to pat the government on the back than they would be when responding to the Minister of Transport.
And, incidentally, is that not a curious situation? We have a Minister of Transport; but the air lines, the stock of which is owned by the C.N.R., report to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. One would think that the Minister of Transport would be responsible for that. It sounds logical. But logic is not always perhaps the thing which we find most evident in this government.
Then, I should like to touch on another point rather briefly. It is that such words as "unethical", "misstatement", "inaccuracies" and "exaggerations" seem suddenly to have become parliamentary-at least they are parliamentary, it would seem, when they are used by the Minister of Transport. I was curious about the point, and took the trouble to look in this little book which contains the standing rules of the house. It will take only a moment to find the rule in question, and I think it should be drawn to the attention of the committee that some of the expressions the minister used when referring to my argument were hardly in line with rule 238 which says:
The imputation of bad motives, or motives different from those acknowledged, misrepresenting the language of another, or accusing him in his turn, of misrepresentation, charging him with falsehood or deceit; or contemptuous or insulting language of any kind; all these are unparliamentary and call for prompt interference,
I was delighted, actually, to see that these words he had used-particularly "unethical" -seemed suddenly to have become parliamentary; because I am sure we will have occasion to use them many times in the future when we are dealing with various actions of this government.
Finally, here is an interesting example of the type of argument the minister used in attempting to refute my argument. He said some rather strong things. He does not think we are qualified-and certainly does not think I am qualified-to deal with his department at all. Well, on that point, I am prepared to go along with the people who elected me. I think if they are reasonably satisfied, I will

stay. And I have much more confidence in their decision as to whether or not I am qualified than I have in that of the minister in the heat of arguing as to the deficiency in his operations.
And let this be my final word. Here, Mr. Chairman, is the minister who has suggested that the full case was not presented in the course of my remarks. He has made that suggestion and that imputation and made that charge. And then, Mr. Chairman, this same individual stands up in this House of Commons and abstracts one paragraph from a group of three paragraphs, abstracts a paragraph which gives the bright side, and ends the quotation there, and omits everything else completely, and absolutely gives a false impression of what this particular man said.
Let us put it on the record, so that we can see the argument that was used tonight in an attempt to show that my case was not as strong as it actually is. The minister had referred to remarks made by Mr. Earle Birney, a Canadian writer and professor of English at the University of British Columbia. The quotation he used was this:
On the credit side I'd say Canadian air terminals are clean with good facilities for telephones, telegraph, enquiry; washrooms good; well heated and ventilated. Passenger handling, baggage, etc., seems fast, courteous, efficient.
The minister stopped there. But as we know, where there is a credit there is a debit. Let us hear what the next paragraph says:
On the debit side, no terminal is big enough. Space is cramped. Seating is inadequate whenever there is a holdup, a general grounding. For example, I waited four hours once in Vancouver airport (Sea island) for ground fog to lift. Winnipeg is even more crowded, and awkwardly cut up. The restaurant is hard to find and too small.
Mr. Birney continued in his article to deal with the delay while repairs were being made to a North Star engine, which I cannot lay at the door of the minister. Later on he continues:
Also, taxi facilities were inadequate and the airport bus had already gone when we found our plane was delayed.
All this was left out by the minister. Mr. Birney continues:
All the airports need public entertainment facilities. Every American airport I've been in had both radio and TV. And nice! There is a civilized airport, with an open air restaurant (windscreened by glass) where you can sit and watch the planes come in and take off, while you have good food, not expensive, and drink what you want, and enjoy the sun if there is any and listen to music. Seattle has an excellent cocktail bar and a view gallery. If we can't have cocktails-but why not?-at least we could have esplanade restaurants, open in summer, where you can wait, eat, watch T.V. and the planes.

I can understand that the minister was making his own case, and I can also understand why he would omit this as well:
Every Canadian airport seems to have been designed to prevent people seeing the planes. Ring in some architects who have imagination and give them some space to play with.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the material that was left out by the minister who had the unmitigated gall to say that I was not giving both sides of the case.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to voice my concern with reference to the many dangerous level railway crossings that exist throughout Canada. I know that this concern has been, and is, in the mind of every citizen of this country, when we realize that the level crossing fatalities are increasing year by year. Yes, these tragic accidents are increasing every month. Boys and girls, young men and women, who are in the vigour of life, and who have many long years and perhaps a magnificent career ahead, are suddenly snuffed out in the midst of life or are maimed and crippled for the remainder of their days.
I had a communication from my constituency on Monday telling of the tragic death of one of our young men in his late twenties who was suddenly snuffed out at a level railway crossing. This crossing is comprised of two lines of tracks, which makes it all the harder for trains to be observed by approaching cars. One train goes by-

Mr. Chairman, I was just leading up to a grievance in my own constituency and the situations that exist there at certain points within the county and within the city of Brockville which I represent. I should like to read from a clipping from the local paper with regard to the lack of signals at this particular railway crossing. The article reads:
The railway crossing is not marked by a wigwag signal nor is there any sign indicating a crossing to northbound motorists.
That proves beyond doubt that the Department of Transport should be more particular in seeing that railroad crossings are properly marked at different intervals. What untold suffering and agony many of our good people are enduring because of those accidents which could have been prevented if only there had been an overhead pass, a subway or some warning signal! I know that many of those fatalities would have been prevented if proper caution had been exercised by the driver of the car or whatever vehicle it might have been. But let us be honest with ourselves. How many of us in this house today or, I may say, how many of us who drive cars have not at some time forgotten and have crossed a railway track or tracks without stopping? When we see so many blind approaches, of which we have many in my own constituency, when we realize there are so many heavily driven roads and highways where the traffic must go over dangerous crossings, and there is no protection whatever, not even a wigwag, gates or signals of any description, it makes us begin to think that we, or some or all of our own families may be the next to suffer that horrible tragedy.
I should like to direct, in as friendly a manner as I can, the attention of the Minister of Transport to a situation that exists at Brockville. The citizens of that city are sadly in need of a subway to carry the heavy traffic under the tracks. It is not only dangerous, but extremely inconvenient. When the east or westbound train comes to a halt at the station it blocks the old highway No. 29 that carries all the traffic to and from Brockville to the north part of the county. And that is not all. It also blocks

what is known as the new Stewart boulevard, which is a portion of highways Nos. 29 and 42. Since the city is expanding north very rapidly the tracks will soon be in the very centre of the town.
On these two heavily travelled roads the cars at times are nearly bumper to bumper. When the traffic is halted for a passenger train to stop at the station, or for a long freight to go through-and they sometimes stop for long intervals because Brockville is a divisional centre-it not only causes many words to be manufactured by the motorists that are not found in the dictionary, but it also frays the nerves of the city and township councils. At times the traffic is halted for long intervals. On one occasion a car was rushing a patient to hospital when it was forced to halt until the train pulled away from the station, and the delay was for some time, but I am glad to say that the mother and child are doing nicely.
There has been so much criticism about blocking the two roads that lately the trains pass beyond the station so as to leave one road open to traffic. This creates a hardship on the passengers, as they must walk and carry their heavy luggage for nearly two blocks back to the station or to the taxis, as the case may be. This does not create a very good impression on the visitors coming to the city. In this connection I would like to quote an article which appeared in a local newspaper on March 10, 1953.

I shall only be a few moments, Mr. Chairman. This letter addressed to the editor of the local newspaper reads as follows:
I wish to make a complaint about the poor system which now exists in Brockville with regard to the stopping of trains at your station.
Being a traveller I have crossed this country from coast to coast and have never experienced such an inconvenience as exists in Brockville. The train stops so far from the station that the passenger is tired out by the time he carries his baggage to the taxis. There is neither porter, red cap nor a convenience to carry one's luggage.
When I arrived in Brockville the other day, the walk from the train to the station was the worst
experience I have ever had and I was compelled to rest quite some time before I began breathing in a normal manner again.

Moral-don't go to
Brockville.

May I suggest that the station master hire a couple of men or boys to carry the passengers' baggage from the train to the station, or perhaps permission could be granted to the taximen to come beyond the west end of the station to get the luggage. Whatever is the answer, something should be done to assist the passengers before someone drops dead on that long trek from the train to the station.
It is only reasonable to expect that Brockville, with a large new industry just completed, another one under construction, and with the deep seaway a reality in the not-too-distant future, will double its present size before too long. Surely the citizens and travelling public are entitled to and should have a safer and speedier way of crossing the tracks on a highway which is used so heavily by trucks and automobiles.
I hope the minister will give this his full consideration, for surely the people of a thriving and growing city like the county town of Leeds are entitled to and should have much better accommodation than they have at the present time. He might contend that subways cost a considerable amount of money, but it is my contention that a subway in this area is long overdue and every possible effort should be made to provide one for where can we spend our money to better advantage than in trying to save the lives of our fellow Canadians.
